title: EXPLAINER: What does chairing IMF, WB boards mean for Pakistan?
text:
• Responsibility returns to Islamabad after 74 years; Ahad Cheema named incoming chair• Board chair’s role ‘mainly procedural and diplomatic, not executive’• Comes with no extra voting power or control over loans and programmes

PAKISTAN has been selected to chair the Boards of Governors of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank Group (WBG) in 2027, marking its return to the position after 74 years.

The chairmanship carries mainly procedural and diplomatic responsibilities and does not give Pakistan additional authority over lending decisions by either institution.

Minister for Economic Affairs Ahad Khan Cheema was announced as the incoming chair during the annual meetings in Bangkok on Oct 16. Pakistan last held the position in 1953, when finance and economic affairs minister Mohammad Ali chaired the eighth annual meetings of the IMF and International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD) in Washington.

Pakistan is not the only South Asian country to have held the chairmanship. India chaired the annual meetings in Paris in 1950, with its finance minister, Chintaman D. Deshmukh, presiding over the proceedings.

Pakistan followed in 1953, Sri Lanka — then known as Ceylon — in 1968 and Nepal in 1999.

The bylaws of the IMF and World Bank set out the procedure for selecting a governor to chair their annual meetings.

Section 6(a) of the World Bank’s bylaws states: “At each annual mee­­t­ing the Board of Governors shall select a Governor to act as Chair.”

The appointment continues until the conclusion of the following annual meeting. Similarly, Section 7 of the IMF’s bylaws provides for the selection of a chair and at least two vice chairs at each regular meeting, with their terms continuing until the next regular meeting.

These provisions establish the selection procedure and duration of the chairmanship, which rotates among member countries, including developing economies, rather than being reserved for major shareholders.

Member countries appoint governors to represent them on the Boards of Governors of the IMF and World Bank. These are generally finance ministers, central bank governors or other senior government officials.

However, the chairmanship is not legally restricted to finance ministers. Any governor appointed by a member country is eligible for selection, regardless of the official position they hold.

Under Section 6(a) of the World Bank’s bylaws and Section 7 of the IMF’s bylaws, the respective boards select their chairs from among these governors. Article V, Section 2(a), of the IBRD Articles of Agreement also provides for the selection of one of its governors as chairman.

In Pakistan, Mr Cheema serves as the country’s governor to the World Bank. Under the Rules of Business, the Economic Affairs Division handles matters relating to the World Bank and other multilateral development institutions, while the Finance Division deals with the IMF.

Historically, the finance minister also held the economic affairs portfolio. However, the two portfolios are currently held by separate ministers, with responsibilities for the World Bank and IMF divided between their respective divisions.

Mr Cheema’s appointment as Pakistan’s governor to the World Bank made him eligible for selection as chair. Pakistan is represented on the IMF Board of Governors by the governor of the State Bank of Pakistan.

However, Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb’s absence from the two Boards of Governors does not diminish his role in Pakistan’s engagement with the institutions. Along with the central bank governor, he continues to lead the country’s economic and financial discussions during the annual meetings.

Under Section 5(d) of the World Bank’s bylaws, the chair, jointly with the bank’s president, is responsible for arrangements concerning meetings of the Board of Governors.

The official Rules of Conduct for Annual Meetings, approved in March 2023, further state: “The Chair of the Boards of Governors will establish the order of speaking at each session.”

The chair may also communicate information about the proceedings to the press alongside the World Bank president and IMF managing director.

However, the chairmanship does not confer executive authority over either institution. Although the Boards of Governors are their highest governing bodies, most operational responsibilities are delegated to their respective Executive Boards.

The position does not give Pakistan additional voting rights, preferential access to financing or authority to approve IMF programmes and World Bank loans.

For Pakistan, the significance of the chairmanship lies mainly in greater international representation and opportunities to engage with senior economic policymakers. It will also provide a platform to contribute to discussions on global economic and development issues, particularly the financing needs of developing countries and the mobilisation of private capital.

Pakistan will preside over the 2027 annual meetings, scheduled for Oct 4-9 in Washington.

The appointment will therefore enhance Pakistan’s diplomatic visibility within the international financial system without changing its voting power or authority over lending decisions.

title: Expensive fuel pushes Sept power costs up 37.5pc
text:
• Average fuel cost jumps to Rs10.02 per unit from Rs7.29 last year• HSD generation cost hits Rs62.14 per unit as use surges• Imported coal share almost doubles to 16.3pc of total generation

ISLAMABAD: Power consumption rose by about four per cent in September from a year earlier, but its fuel cost surged by almost 37.5pc, mainly because high-tax-laden expensive fuels were used to compensate for war-related constraints on liquefied natural gas (LNG) supplies and greater reliance on imported coal.

Data reported by the Central Power Purchasing Agency (CPPA) to the National Electric Power Regulatory Authority (Nepra) put the average fuel cost at Rs10.022 per unit in September 2026 against Rs7.29 per unit a year earlier, showing an increase of Rs2.74 per unit, or 37.48pc.

However, data also revealed that power consumption in September was down by about 12pc compared to August, while the fuel cost increased by 13.5pc to Rs10.022 per unit from Rs8.83.

The CPPA also reported generation of about 213 gigawatt hours (GWh) from high-speed diesel (HSD), or around 1.6pc of total grid supply, after many months of limited use. Its generation cost reached a record Rs62.14 per unit compared to Rs54 per unit in August, when HSD-based generation stood at only 80GWh.

Furnace oil-based generation cost dropped slightly to Rs44.86 per unit in September, with output of 263GWh, against about Rs46 per unit in August, when generation stood at 321GWh. Its share in overall grid supply remained almost unchanged at around 2pc.

Ironically, furnace oil carries around Rs75,000 per tonne in taxes on domestic consumption under IMF requirements, even though it is produced locally and surplus output is exported at a discount. The CPPA has publicly expressed its inability to reduce or waive taxes and duties on furnace oil despite seeking lower power generation costs.

Two major factors contributed to the price shock, prompting the CPPA to seek an additional fuel cost adjustment of about Rs2.5624 per unit from consumers.

These included lower RLNG-based generation, which fell to about 804GWh in September from 1,815GWh in the same month last year, and lower nuclear generation, which declined to 1,893GWh from 2,227GWh.

The decline in nuclear output was mainly due to the prolonged return of nuclear power plants from refuelling and technical repairs. However, nuclear generation improved from 1,528GWh in August as plants returned to service.

As a consequence, the share of imported coal-based generation almost doubled to 16.3pc in September from 8pc in the same month last year. Output from imported coal rose to 2,155GWh from 1,019GWh.

The generation cost from imported coal also increased by about 25.5pc to Rs17.24 per unit compared to Rs13.74 per unit in September last year.

The increase in overall generation cost came despite about 76pc of electricity produced in September coming from domestic sources that are either che­a­per or carry little or no fuel cost.

These included hydropower, which contributed around 37pc of generation at zero fuel cost, and domestic coal, with a share of about 10pc at around Rs6 per unit compared to Rs13 per unit a year earlier.

In addition, local gas, nuclear and renewables contributed about 29pc share to the national grid at almost unchanged fuel costs. Last year, supplies from these domestic sources were slightly higher, at around 76.5pc.

title: Naqvi assails politico upset over not getting KP governorship
text:
LAHORE: Interior Min­ister Mohsin Naqvi on Fri­day claimed that the “head of a party” was “extremely upset” over not being app­ointed governor of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

“The head of a party is extremely upset over being denied a role in the new setup in KP and not getting the governorship,” Mr Naqvi claimed, while speaking to journalists in Lahore.

Although he did not name anyone, observers bel­ieve he was alluding to JUI-F chief Maulana Faz­lur Rehman, who has been critical of the federal government over the imposition of governor’s rule in KP.

The minister alleged that this politician had remained “dependent on the establishment for decades to advance his political career”.

“These are the same politicians who remained in politics for decades with the support of the establishment, and this politician even relied on the establishment to arrange air tickets for the members of his party,” he further alleged.

He said such politicians had little justification for criticising others after benefiting from the same system they now denounced.

“Political differences are part of politics. However, instead of using inappropriate language and making allegations, political leaders should speak on the basis of arguments and facts,” the minister added.

Mr Naqvi’s remarks came days after the Centre imposed governor’s rule and emergency in KP, citing the provincial government’s “deliberate disengagement” from the fight against terrorism.

In the days preceding the move, political tensions between the Centre and the opposition, including the PTI-led KP government, had remained high after jailed former prime minister Imran Khan’s party announced a protest march to Islamabad to demand his release.

Intense negotiations between the two sides a week before the imposition of governor’s rule failed to yield results, while the Maulana was seen as someone who could help defuse tensions between the Centre and the PTI. Both sides reportedly held separate meetings with the JUI-F chief to seek his intervention in breaking the deadlock.

After the federal government imposed governor’s rule in KP, the Maulana accused the Centre of reneging on its commitments despite his mediation efforts.

On Thursday, the JUI-F chief again criticised the federal government, accusing it of depriving provinces of their rights. Addressing a rally in Multan, he recalled that his party had expressed reservations over the merger of the former tribal areas with KP under the 25th Constitutional Amendment in 2018.

“We were not against the merger, but we said that it was an issue of the political future of the people of tribal areas,” he said, alleging that residents had not been consulted.

Questioning the Centre’s justification for imposing governor’s rule on the grounds of inadequate cooperation in counterterrorism efforts, he said the security situation in Balochistan was worse than in KP.

He alleged that governor’s rule had not been imposed in Balochistan because the province’s chief minister “praises you”.

“In KP, the PTI is in power. […] Where opposition is in power, you topple it. And the resources of former tribal areas, which had become part of the province, you have taken control of them by imposing emergency,” he remarked.

During his interaction with journalists on Friday, Mr Naqvi also spoke about the former tribal areas, questioning concerns over the allocation of resources to the merged districts.

“When the [merged] districts … were not getting their rightful share for years, why were these people silent?” he asked.

The minister said political leaders had failed to speak out for the rights of people in the former tribal areas and stressed that their rights and resources should be treated as an issue above political

Mr Naqvi further said KP was facing serious security challenges and urged political leaders to play a constructive role in restoring peace and combating terrorism.

“Instead of fanning the flames and creating unrest, political leaders should play their role in restoring law and order and eliminating terrorism,” he said, adding that the province needed peace, stability and collective efforts rather than political confrontation.

Separately, Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz criticised the JUI-F chief in a post on X.

She said it was not expected of a senior politician such as him to support those who facilitated terrorism, an apparent reference to the PTI, which the Centre accuses of backing terrorism.

She added that it was unfortunate that he was supporting the party instead of holding accountable those she blamed for KP’s decline due to “incompetence, ineptitude and corruption”.

She also criticised the Maulana for his remarks about Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir, apparently referring to his comments at the Multan rally about the centralisation of power.

The Punjab CM concluded by saying that the PTI alone was “responsible for the end of its government in KP”.

title: Islamabad backs Riyadh, with an eye on diplomacy
text:
• PM vows to safeguard Saudi sovereignty and security; condemns deadly Houthi attacks• FO says Pakistan will honour its defence obligation; leaves question of military action to Makkah alliance• Coalition intercepts drones, missiles over Riyadh; fighting rages on Taiz front

ISLAMABAD: Pakistan on Friday reaffirmed its support for Saudi Arabia’s security and said it would fulfil its obligations under their defence agreements after a wave of lethal Houthi missile and drone attacks on the kingdom, even as it insisted the war in Yemen had no military solution.

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said that Pakistan stood with Saudi Arabia in safeguarding its “sovereignty, security and territorial integrity”, while strongly condemning a recent escalation in Houthi attacks that has killed and injured civilians, including Pakistani nationals.

His comments came during a meeting in Islamabad with Saudi Arabia’s newly appointed ambassador to Pakistan, Dr Rajeh Tami Albugamy.

PM Shehbaz welcomed the envoy and congratulated him on taking up his diplomatic assignment, saying relations between Islamabad and Riyadh had made significant progress in recent years and that Pakistan wanted to deepen cooperation across a range of sectors.

He said Pakistan and Saudi Arabia had historically supported one another and described their Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement and the Makkah Joint Defence Alliance as historic milestones in their relationship and a reflection of their commitment to regional security.

The prime minister also thanked the Saudi leadership for its longstanding economic and financial support for Pakistan and assured Albugamy of Islamabad’s cooperation in strengthening bilateral ties.

In a separate meeting, the ambassador held talks with Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister, Ishaq Dar, who emphasised the longstanding fraternal and strategic relationship between the two countries.

Mr Dar reaffirmed their “shared commitment to further strengthen bilateral cooperation for mutual progress and prosperity”.

Mr Albugamy conveyed greetings from the Saudi leadership, while Mr Dar sent his best wishes to Saudi King Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and other Saudi leaders.

The prime minister’s remarks were reinforced by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs at its weekly briefing, where the spokesperson cited Saudi Arabia’s right to defend its sovereignty under Article 51 of the UN Charter.

“Pakistan is a party to the bilateral defence agreement with Saudi Arabia, and a trilateral arrangement is also in place,” Foreign Office spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan told reporters on Friday.

“Pakistan will fulfil its obligations under these agreements.”

The FO said the secretariat of the Makkah alliance was being established and that its secretary-general had already been appointed. It also condemned the latest attack on King Khalid international airport in Riyadh.

The injured Pakistanis were receiving treatment at different locations in Riyadh, the foreign ministry said, adding that Pakistan’s diplomatic mission was in contact with them and their families.

“Attacks against civilian populations and critical infrastructure are unacceptable and constitute a grave threat to regional peace and security,” the spokesperson said, reiterating Pakistan’s commitment to Saudi Arabia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.

However, when pressed on when Islamabad’s treaty commitments might cross the threshold into direct military action, the foreign ministry declined to be drawn into operational specifics.

Any deployment or military response, the spokesperson said, was a matter for Pakistan’s armed forces, the military’s media wing, and the general secretariat of the Makkah alliance in Riyadh to address.

Despite its defence commitments to Riyadh, Pakistan also stressed its support for Yemen’s sovereignty, territorial integrity, unity and independence and said the conflict could not ultimately be resolved militarily.

“There is no solution through war,” the spokesperson said. “Peace can only be restored through negotiations and the peaceful settlement of disputes.”

Islamabad said it remained committed to diplomacy and de-escalation and supported regional and international efforts aimed at finding a lasting political settlement.

The FO also condemned threats to commercial shipping in the Red Sea and expressed concern over the humanitarian and maritime consequences of the widening conflict.

The violence intensified in Yemen on Friday, with Aden, the interim capital of the Saudi-backed and internationally recognised government, coming under missile attack.

Authorities said two missiles landed within the perimeter of Aden airport, while the Houthis claimed responsibility for the attack.

In a statement attributed to a military source, the group said it had targeted what it described as the Saudi forces’ command headquarters at Badr camp in Aden province, as well as a weapons depot.

Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis also reported that it had intercepted three drones over Riyadh and southern Saudi Arabia, as well as two cruise missiles over the Red Sea. Coalition spokesperson Turki al-Malki said a ballistic missile had also been intercepted over Yanbu, a Red Sea city that hosts the terminus of a major oil pipeline.

Fighting has also continued around Taiz, where forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognised government have been trying to halt Houthi advances.

Government media reported that forces had repelled Houthi attacks on the Dhahih and Hisn Kahlan fronts, while clashes continued around Jabal al-Dahhih in Taiz province’s al-Masrakh district, according to Al Jazeera.

Iran on Friday denied Saudi accusations that it was involved in the Houthis’ recent escalation against the kingdom.

The denial came after Saudi deputy minister for public diplomacy Rayed Krimly earlier this week accused Iran of continuing “to arm, train and support the Houthis” and of encouraging the group’s attacks.

title: Two killed in Turbat ‘shooting’ incident
text:
GWADAR: Two people  were killed in an alleged shooting incident inside a house in Doctor Colony, Turbat, according to official sources.

Initial reports suggest that the incident occurred following a dispute between armed individuals.

The deceased were identified as Sarfaraz, a resident of Shahi Tump, and Aamir, a resident of Sariab, Quetta.

Police confirmed the incident and said Sarfaraz, also known as Mulla Sarfaraz, was a proclaimed offender wanted in connection with a murder case.

His body was handed over to his family after the necessary formalities, while Aamir’s body is to be transported to Quetta.

title: Balochistan girl wins FAO award in Italy
text:
QUETTA: A young girl from Awaran district of Balochistan has won the 100 Women Heroes Award 2026 of United Nations Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) in Rome, Italy.

Aqsa Mirwani, a farmer, social entrepreneur and community leader from tehsil Jahoo of Awaran district, was presented the award by FAO Director General QU Dongyu at a ceremony held in Rome that marked the ‘International Year of the Woman Farmer 2026’.

Ms Mirwani was the only Pakistani among participants from 131 countries.

The FAO’s 100 Women Heroes initiative recognises women from across the agrifood value chain and rural development who are helping expand opportunities, strengthen food security, preserve knowledge, protect natural resources and create opportunities for rural communities. The international accolade recognises Ms Mirwani’s contributions to rural development and her role in transforming agrifood systems. Her achievement is being hailed as a historic milestone for women in Balochistan.

title: Ten terrorists nabbed in separate Balochistan IBOs
text:
QUETTA: Balochistan government officials said on Friday that six terrorists affiliated with the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), two would-be female suicide bombers, and two commanders of a banned organisation had been arrested during intelligence-based operations across the province.

They said around 90 arrested terrorists were being held at a centre where investigations and legal proceedings were underway.

This was stated by Shahid Rind, adviser to the Balochistan chief minister on media and political aff­airs, during a media briefing alongside Additional Chief Secretary Hamza Shafqaat and Quetta DIG Imran Shaukat.

Mr Rind said police, security forces and other law enforcement agencies had conducted intelligence-based operations across Balochistan, killing several terrorists and prompting others to surrender to the state. He said two commanders of a banned organisation had been arrested in Shaban and Khadkocha, along with six TTP terrorists and two would-be female suicide bombers.

CM’s aide says six TTP terrorists, two would-be female suicide bombers and two commanders of a banned outfit arrested

Mr Rind said the state remained willing to give those who abandoned militancy and accepted Pakistan’s Constitution and laws an opportunity to return to normal life. He cited the example of Shahab, a resident of Panjgur, who had reportedly joined a banned organisation through social media.

He said the government had introduced programmes to encourage young people who had joined armed groups to abandon militancy and return to mainstream society with the help of their families, political representatives and district administrations.

Mr Rind said counterterrorism operations would continue in coordination with the federal

government under the provincial action plan.

Mr Shafqaat said the Counter-Terrorism Department (CTD) and security forces had arrested Niaz Jatoi and Habibur Rehman, residents of Kardgap, in August following a heightened threat alert. He said their arrests had foiled a planned terrorist attack in Quetta on Aug 14 as part of “Herof-3”.

Weapons and explosives, including hand grenades and light mac­hine guns, allegedly being transported from Chagai to Quetta, were recovered, while the vehicles inv­olved were also seized, he added.

Mr Shafqaat said the provincial government had enacted 16 laws and established 17 departments over the past two years. He added that rehabilitation efforts were also underway for detained militants, citing previous cases in which individuals, including Khadija Baloch, had been rehabilitated and reunited with their families.

DIG Imran Shaukat said the CTD and other law enforcement agencies had conducted 3,300 intelligence-based operations across Balochistan, arresting more than 300 suspected terrorists and killing hundreds.

He said police capacity had been strengthened, but two security personnel had been killed in the ongoing fight against terrorism.

Video statements by Shahab, Niaz Jatoi and Habibur Rehman were also played during the briefing.

title: Slain teacher’s family protests in Pasni
text:
GWADAR: The family of slain schoolteacher Parvez Mazar and a large number of people staged a protest rally outside the Pasni Press Club, demanding the arrest of the suspects nominated in the FIR.

A large number of women and children also participated in the demonstration, carrying placards and photographs of the deceased schoolteacher.

According to family members, Parvez Mazar was allegedly abducted and tortured before being murdered.

Participants demanded that the suspects nominated in the FIR be handed over to police instead of being provided shelter. They demanded justice for the victim’s family. The protesters said that incidents of kidnapping, murder and bullet-riddled bodies were creating resentment against members of security forces and state institutions among the masses and the situation required immediate attention and an end to this state of insecurity and lawlessness in the province.

title: Terrorism has no link with Baloch values, says Bugti
text:
QUETTA: Condemning a recent terrorist attack in Dasht Goran, Balochistan Chief Minister Mir Sarfraz Bugti said on Friday that the government had always maintained that such acts have nothing to do with Baloch values, rather were purely terrorism.

He was responding to points raised by lawmakers on various issues in the Balochistan Assembly.

Earlier, MPA Mir Jahanzeb Mengal, speaking on a point of order, said that “Fitna al-Hindustan” had attacked the house of Mir Qambar Khan Mengal in Dasht Goran at 6am. He said the firing continued until 4pm, leaving Ahmed Nawaz Mengal dead and another person injured.

“This is my house, and my mother and sisters are there. This is not Balochiyat. If anyone is so keen on fighting, let them specify the place, field and time. The Balochistan chief minister should take notice of the incident,” he said.

Condemns Dasht Goran attack; directs district administrations to inspect school and college buildings in Balochistan

CM Bugti said the people of the province were increasingly realising that the Baloch were being pushed into a futile conflict. “What kind of tradition allows the killing of passengers and unarmed people?” he asked.

Then, speaking about the high-profile Asma Jattak case, he said the government had been in contact with her family.

“I have said before that the matter is sensitive and cannot be discussed on the floor of the assembly,” he said.

The case he was referring to revolves around the murder of Ms Jattak’s father in August this year. The woman in question was abducted in 2025. After being freed, she levelled allegations against an influential individual, accusing him of threatening her family. The same day, her father was shot dead outside their residence.

Referring to remarks by lawmakers during a previous sitting, the chief minister said it was inappropriate to name an individual, whose father had also served as the provincial chief minister, and allege on the assembly floor that those responsible for the killing of Asma Jattak’s father were present in the house.

“I have reports from the security agencies, and the information provided by the member concerned is incorrect,” he said.

Referring to the recent school roof collapse incident in Peshawar where several children lost their lives, former chief minister Dr Abdul Malik Baloch urged the chief minister to direct the Education Department, the Communications and Works (C&W) Department and local councillors to inspect all government and private school buildings across Balochistan.

He said officials should visit schools in every area and ensure that any building found to be dilapidated was closed until it could be made safe.

In response, the chief minister said he had directed authorities to inspect the buildings of all schools and colleges across the province.

Speaker Abdul Khaliq Khan Achak­­zai noted that because madressahs accommodate children, their buildings also require strict safety inspections.

title: Inner Temple welcomes CJP Afridi as Honorary Bencher
text:
ISLAMABAD: The So­­ciety of the Inner Temple in the United Kingdom has welcomed Chief Justi­ce of Pakistan (CJP) Yahya Afridi as an Honorary Bencher at its Benchers’ Night in London.

The occasion provided an opportunity to explore ways to strengthen institutional cooperation between the judicial and legal institutions of Pakistan and the United Kingdom through the exchange of knowledge, experience and professional expertise, according to a press release.

Discussions focused on judicial capacity-building, particularly in case management and judgement writing, as well as opportunities to enhance professional standards in legal ethics and advocacy. These areas offer scope for closer engagement and mutual learning between the two jurisdictions.

Continued institutional cooperation can facilitate the exchange of best practices, strengthen judicial skills and promote professionalism within the legal community.

The Chief Justice’s association with the Inner Temple as an Honorary Bencher provides a valuable link for fostering these exchanges and further strengthening ties betwe­­en the legal communities of Pakistan and the United Kingdom.

title: Imaan, Hadi and their counsel walk out of jail trial in protest
text:
RAWALPINDI: Rights activist and lawyer Imaan Zainab Mazari-Hazir and her husband, Hadi Ali Chattha, on Friday objected to the manner in which they were presented during the hearing of the security breach case, with the couple and their lawyers eventually walking out of the proceedings at Adiala jail.

The defence counsel also filed an application seeking an end to the jail trial. The case pertains to the alleged disruption of a security route for an international cricket team and incitement to public unrest. Ms Mazari and her husband have been accused of removing barriers from the route and were  indicted on Oct 7.

A day earlier, following police concerns about transport limitations, an Islamabad anti-terrorism court (ATC) directed lawyers and witnesses to appear at Adiala jail for the next hearing.

On Friday, ATC Judge Tahir Abbas Sipra conducted the hearing inside Adiala jail. The accused were presented in a dock in a corner of the courtroom, prompting objections.

“This is not the proper way to present someone in court,” Ms Mazari said, adding that they were not being allowed to meet their lawyers. Mr Chattha complained that they were being treated worse than terrorists.

At this, Judge Sipra directed police personnel standing next to the accused to move away.

“They [the couple] have been brought into the courtroom; what is the need for the police to stand right next to them?” the judge remarked.

The defence also filed an application seeking an end to the jail trial and an adjournment of the hearing. After hearing arguments, the court announced a 20-minute recess.

After proceedings resumed, prosecution witness Ibrahim recorded his statement, while defence lawyer Aimal Khan Mandokhail urged the court to decide the adjournment application before proceeding further.

“We have filed an application to adjourn the hearing; please rule on it,” he said. He also complained that other members of the defence team were not being allowed to enter the courtroom.

“If the proceedings continue in this manner, we cannot remain a part of them,” Mr Mandokhail said. He urged the court not to defer the matter until the following day, referring to the pending bail proceedings. Subsequently, the couple and their lawyers walked out of the courtroom.

Meanwhile, Margaret Satterth­waite, the UN special rapporteur on the independence of judges and lawyers, expressed deep concern over the reported denial of access to lawyers for Ms Mazari and Mr Chattha and their objections to the jail trial.

“Jail trials must not undermine fair trial guarantees, access to counsel or the effective right to defence,” she wrote in a post on X.

“Criminal charges should never be used as punishment for freedom of expression and human rights advocacy.”

title: SC questions ‘lofty expectations’ in criminal cases
text:
ISLAMABAD: The Supreme Court has taken exception to a prevalent practice in criminal trials which, it said, defied normal human capability and natural perception, and observed that eyewitness accounts should reflect genuine human observation rather than physically impossible details concerning firearm incidents.

“To expect mathematical precision regarding the number of firearm shots or the exact location of injuries from eyewitnesses exposed to a horrific event is both unnatural and impractical,” observed Justice Ishtiaq Ibrahim in a judgement he authored.

Justice Ibrahim was a member of a three-judge SC bench headed by Justice Muhammad Hashim Khan Kakar, which took up criminal appeals filed by Muhammad Azhar and the state challenging a Sept 13, 2021, Lahore High Court, Bahawalpur, ruling.

The SC, however, rejected the criminal appeal in the 2017 murder case, upholding Muhammad Azhar’s conviction for killing Sakhian Bibi.

Expecting mathematical precision from eyewitnesses exposed to traumatic events is ‘unnatural and impractical’, Justice Ibrahim holds

“In criminal jurisprudence, human behaviour should not be subjected to a fixed formula, nor should every witness be expected to react to, observe or retain events in an identical manner,” the judgement said.

The incident occurred on Jan 11, 2017, when the appellant allegedly entered the victim’s home armed with a .30-bore pistol, seeking the complainant’s uncle in connection with ongoing civil litigation. When the victim said her uncle was not present, the petitioner opened fire, discharging five shots that struck her chest, abdomen and right arm.

The additional sessions judge, Minch­inabad, convicted the petitioner and sentenced him to death, with Rs200,000 in compensation payable to the legal heirs. The LHC, Bahawalpur, later commuted the death sentence to life imprisonment, prompting both the petitioner’s appeal and the state’s petition for enhancement of the sentence.

“We frequently observe prosecution witnesses deposing with microscopic precision, as if watching events in slow motion, describing the exact trajectory and anatomical landing site of each individual bullet discharged from a firearm,” the judgement observed. It is humanly impossible for an eyewitness exposed to the sudden terror and high stress of a deadly attack to track a high-velocity bullet in mid-air and confirm precisely where each shot strikes the victim’s body, it noted.

The judge emphasised that every individual reacts differently to a sudden traumatic situation: while one person may observe details, another may freeze or lose awareness of the occurrence. In a sudden traumatic event, when multiple gunshots ring out within a few seconds and a mother is murdered in cold blood before her son’s eyes, a minor divergence regarding the exact number of firearm shots or the precise entry point of each bullet is evidence of natural and reasonable human limitations, he observed.

It is common knowledge that most individuals are not frequently exposed to dangerous, life-threatening situations, and the sudden brandishing of a weapon induces an atmosphere of shock and fear, according to the judgement.

In such stressful encounters, human cognitive and perceptual capacities are severely impaired, the judgement said. To substantiate this point, it cited renowned cognitive psychologist Elizabeth Loftus, who had stated that a witness confronted by an assailant brandishing a firearm involuntarily fixes their attention almost exclusively on the weapon itself. This cognitive phenomenon, known as “attentional tunnelling”, limits the observer’s capacity to process or recall surrounding details, the judgement said.

Trial courts should bear these limitations in mind when scrutinising eyewitness accounts claiming microscopic accuracy despite the stressful circumstances, Justice Ibrahim observed.

The judgement expected lower courts to assess witnesses in the light of the circumstances of each case, observing that, under the golden principles of criminal jurisprudence, no piece of evidence should be considered in isolation; rather, all evidence should be evaluated cumulatively alongside other available evidence.

title: Tempers cool in NA after heated couple of days
text:
ISLAMABAD: The lower house of parliament witnessed lacklustre proceedings on Friday, with only three federal ministers in attendance, after two days of bustling National Assembly sessions to approve the proclamation of emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

While it was expected that senior government and opposition lea­­ders would continue their hea­ted speeches on the proclamation of emergency and governor’s rule, not a single MNA from either side of the aisle spoke on the matter.

The proceedings began at 11.35am, over half an hour behind schedule, with around 50 to 60 MNAs — including Defence Minister Khawaja Asif, Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar and Minister for Parliamentary Affairs Tariq Fazal Chaudhry from the treasury benches and fewer than 15 opposition members — present in the house.

Leader of the Opposition Mahmood Achakzai and the top PTI leadership were absent.

It was expected that the law minister would speak on the floor of the house if any opposition member raised the issue of emergency and governor’s rule in KP. However, as no lawmaker spoke on the matter, the law minister also remained silent.

The proclamation of emerge­n­­cy in KP was endorsed by the Nat­ional Assembly and the Senate on Wednesday, while governor’s rule was approved by a joint sitting of the two houses on Thursday. All these sessions witnessed heavy attendance by lawmakers.

During Question Hour, the decline in tourism in Pakistan overshadowed proceedings when PPP MNA Dr Nafisa Shah raised the issue of the lack of interest shown by foreign tourists in visiting the country.

Referring to official figures, she said the highest number of foreign tourists came from Afgha­nistan, followed by the United Kingdom. “It is a big question that the highest number of tourists came from Afghanistan,” she added.

“Despite having a precious he­­ritage and the more than 6,000-year-old Gandhara and Taxila civilisations, we have failed to attract foreign tourists and earn foreign exchange,” she noted.

In response, Parliamentary Sec­retary for Inter-Provincial Coor­di­nation Kiran Dar failed to satisfy the questioner and even Deputy Sp­­eaker Syed Ghulam Mustafa Shah. The deputy speaker said the ministry could not distinguish betw­een Afghan refugees and tourists.

The house was also informed that the number of qualified Pakistanis seeking immigration to foreign countries had declined significantly.

title: FBI alerts Sikh leader to life threat ahead of anti-India vote
text:
WASHINGTON: The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has warned Sikh separatist leader Gurpatwant Singh Pannun of an imminent threat to his life, days before he is due to attend a pro-Khalistan referendum in Edmonton, Canada, according to Pannun.

Pannun, a dual American-Canadian citizen and general counsel of Sikhs for Justice (SFJ), told CBS News on October 15 that FBI agents had visited his New York City home to alert him to the threat. The FBI is investigating the reported threats, CBS News reported.

According to Pannun, the FBI issued a “Duty to Warn” notification on October 15, particularly concerning his planned travel to Canada for the October 18 referendum. SFJ says the event will proceed as scheduled.

Pannun has also reported receiving warnings from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) about threats to his life and his residence in Ontario.

The warnings come as Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi seek to strengthen bilateral relations through negotiations for a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) and greater cooperation on security and law enforcement.

The renewed engagement follows tensions over allegations of Indian involvement in threats against Sikh separatist activists in Canada and the United States. Questioning Ottawa’s approach, Pannun said closer economic and security ties with New Delhi raised questions about Canada’s response to threats against Khalistan referendum organisers.

“How can Canada claim progress on security cooperation with India while assassination threats against Khalistan Referendum activists continue on Canadian soil?” he asked.

Pannun also questioned whether the reported threats reflected a change in the Indian government’s conduct or in Canada’s approach to confronting them.

He was previously the target of a foiled assassination plot in the United States in 2023. US prosecutors brought a criminal case involving an alleged plot directed by a former Indian intelligence official, drawing attention to allegations of transnational repression targeting Sikh separatists.

The June 2023 assassination of Sikh activist Hardeep Singh Nijjar in Surrey, British Columbia, further strained relations between Canada and India. Canadian authorities have pursued allegations related to the killing, while India has denied involvement in violence against Sikh activists abroad.

SFJ says other referendum organizers in Canada have also received warnings in recent months, including organizers in Ontario and British Columbia. Avtar Singh Pannu, an American referendum coordinator, was reportedly warned of a threat to his life while visiting Edmonton.

SFJ plans to hold a non-binding Khalistan referendum in Edmonton on October 18, asking participants whether Punjab should become independent from India and be established as Khalistan.

title: 30 die in drone strike on market in Sudan
text:
KHARTOUM: A drone strike on a cattle market in Sudan’s Nyala killed 30 people on Friday, a medical source said, in one of the deadliest attacks on the paramilitary stronghold in the western Darfur region.

The Rapid Support Forces blamed the attack on the army, while a military source acknowledged an uptick in strikes on the area, without claiming responsibility.

Both the RSF and the army, at war since April 2023, have increasingly used drones to launch far-reaching attacks without sacrificing their fighters.

Nyala, Sudan’s second-largest city and the capital of South Darfur state, serves as the seat of the self-declared administration established by the RSF last year.

“The drone strike on the city’s cattle market today killed 30 people and wounded 47 others, who are receiving treatment at the hospital,” a medical source at Nyala Hospital said.

The source did not say who was responsible for the attack.

title: Wife of UK official backs Palestine Action in social media post
text:
LONDON: British police said on Friday they were assessing a social media post after the wife of National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell appeared to express support for Palestine Action, a pro-Palestinian group banned by London.

Journalist and author Sarah Helm, who is married to Powell, responded on X to a post about the Irish novelist Sally Rooney, who this week announced her books would no longer be sold in Britain over her plans to use her royalties to support Palestine Action.

Helm said in the post: “God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action.”

In response, a police spokesperson said the post is  “being assessed to determine whether any further police investigation may be required”.

Since Palestine Action was proscribed last year, expressing support for the group constitutes a criminal offence.

Asked for comment, a government spokeswoman said:  “These views are held by an individual who does not represent the government in any capacity.”

Palestine Action has carried out protests in support of Palestinian causes.

Amnesty International says more than 3,500 people have been arrested in Britain for alleged support of Palestine Action since it was banned last year, many of them for holding up placards.

Palestine Action challenged the British government’s decision to ban the group, but the Court of Appeal ruled in June that the proscription was lawful.

title: Teenager kills three children, teacher at school in Oregon
text:
BEND: A 16-year-old boy shot dead three children and a teacher at an elementary school in the US state of Oregon on Thursday, jolting police into examining how he got hold of the long gun used in his attack.

The latest deadly school shooting in the United States unfolded when the teenager, who has not been publicly identified, shot through a locked door at Silver Rail Elementary School in central Oregon, according to  police.

The teenager killed three children aged five, eight and 11 and one teacher before he himself was shot dead by an armed bystander who had pursued him into the school, police chief Mike Krantz said at a press conference.

Such shootings have become common in the US, with each one reviving debate over gun laws in a country where a right to “keep and bear arms” is protected under the constitution.

The bystander was not identified by police, although the New York Times reported that he was the father of two girls who attend the school.

Oregon Governor Tina Kotek said at the press conference that the bystander “heroically intervened to stop further loss of life”.

Beyond those killed, a seven-year-old student and a 54-year-old teacher were taken to hospital with critical injuries.

It was not clear if the shooter had any prior connection to the school, which has about 450 students from kindergarten through the fifth grade, roughly ages five to 11, and 40 staff members.

The New York Times, citing unnamed law enforcement officials, identified the teenager as John J. Griffin II, and investigators searched his home and seized electronic devices. They believe he used a 12-gauge pump-action Maverick 88 shotgun in the attack, which police say is registered to his mother.

Some of the deadliest school attacks in the US include those at Columbine High School in 1999, Sandy Hook Elementary School in 2012, Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in 2018 and Robb Elementary School in Uvalde, Texas, in 2022.

Advocates for gun-owners’ rights have argued for arming teachers as a means of defence. The Gun Owners of America advocacy group pointed to the armed bystander’s intervention in Bend as evidence for their position.

title: Israeli settlers attack US photographer covering violence in West Bank
text:
RAMALLAH: Israeli settlers beat an American photojournalist working for The Washington Post on Friday while she was covering ongoing violence against Palestinian olive farmers in the occupied West Bank.

Heidi Levine, a veteran photographer, was taken to hospital in Ramallah following the attack, with photos showing her lying on a gurney with injuries to her leg and hand.

The incident comes 10 days after settlers beat an AFP photographer covering the olive harvest, Jaafar Ashtiyeh, leaving him also requiring hospital treatment.

Speaking to journalists from her hospital bed, Levine said that “more than 50” masked settlers holding sticks suddenly attacked her while she was working near the Palestinian villages of Abu Falah and Turmus Ayya.

“All of a sudden they jumped at me and I luckily had my helmet and flak jacket on. I kept my face to the ground to try to protect my face,” she said.

“They just kept kicking me and kicking me,” she added.

The Washington Post reported that Levine had been wearing a flak jacket with “Press” clearly marked on the front and back.

A spokesman for the US embassy said it was aware of reports of the attack, declining to comment further due to privacy laws.

“We have no higher responsibility than protecting American citizens,” he said.

An eyewitness said he saw Palestinian medics tending to someone on the ground and Israeli soldiers pushing away journalists trying to approach.

The Israeli military said troops and police were deployed to the area “following a report of a violent confrontation”. “Foreign media personnel were present at the scene and a female journalist had been injured during the confrontation,” it said, adding the circumstances would be examined.

“Attacks and violence against innocent civilians are grave and unacceptable acts,” the military said.

The Israeli police said it had opened an investigation into incidents in Abu Falah and Turmus Ayya.

“We were on our land, picking olives, and suddenly the settlers came down on us and started hitting us, throwing stones,” said Mukhllis Zuhdi, a farmer from Abu Falah.

“There was even a foreign journalist whom they beat. These people have no mercy or compassion in their hearts,” he said.

The Foreign Press Association, which represents international media in Israel and the Palestinian territories, said the settlers stole Levine’s passport, phone, wallet and equipment.

“This is the latest in a long line of violent attacks by Israeli settlers against journalists and other civilians in the occupied West Bank,” it said.

“Yet our repeated calls for action to confront this lawlessness have been ignored by Israeli authorities,” it added.

Reporters Without Borders said it strongly condemned the attack and called on Israeli authorities to “put an end to this impunity and prosecute the perpetrators of this heinous assault”.

“This brazen violence is evidence of the impunity with which extremist Jewish settlers operate, often under the protection of Israeli armed forces,” added the advocacy group, known by its French initials RSF.

Violence has flared in recent months in occupied West Bank, with near-daily attacks, thefts or vandalism by Israeli settlers against Palestinians.

Settlers have also been seizing olive groves owned by Palestinians, who see the trees as a cultural symbol.

Excluding east Jerusalem, around three million Palestinians live in occupied West Bank, alongside more than 500,000 Israelis residing in settlements considered illegal under international law.

title: Trump’s new press secretary out after less than a week
text:
WASHINGTON: White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia was pushed out on Friday after less than a week in the

high-profile job, following a series of blunders that added to distractions for her embattled boss, President Donald Trump.

“Can confirm”, a White House official said, after Fox News reported that Zacharia, 41, was “transitioning out”. The writing was on the wall earlier when Trump made clear he was ready to see his newly minted spokeswoman go amid criticism that she had pretended to be a lawyer and over her one, much-mocked press briefing.

“I said, ‘Katie, is this for you?’” Trump told reporters. “I said, ‘Katie, you don’t have to do this’... I said to her, ‘Honestly if I were you I’d reconsider.’”

Zacharia only began her job five days ago, taking over from the combative Karoline Leavitt, who helped Trump reshape White House coverage by bringing in more friendly outlets and fiercely attacking critical media.

Zacharia had got off to a rocky start with her debut press room briefing on Tuesday morning.

It lasted less than 15 minutes, beginning with a remarkably slow reading out of what she said were Trump’s many accomplishments, then taking just three questions from journalists.

She then was plunged into controversy when it emerged that her previous claims to be a lawyer were not true.

The kerfuffle is a distraction for 80-year-old Trump as he flies around the country trying to boost Republican candidates ahead of the November 3 congressional midterm elections, with polls predicting a drubbing.

Zacharia had described herself as a lawyer during television appearances and on social media, and listed herself as general counsel of a California-based conservative nonprofit.

While she does have a law degree from a California university, she acknowledged Thursday she had failed the bar exam, a prerequisite for practising law in the United States.

She embarked on a series of damage-control interviews on Trump-friendly outlets, but they did no good.

In one of them, Sean Hannity of Fox News appeared dismissive of Zacharia.

He asked the press secretary if she ever retook the bar exam. She replied: “I did not.”

“It was never my intent to go into the practice of law,” she said.

title: Official says Trump didn’t order curb on Starshield
text:
WASHINGTON: Donald Trump did not request a reduction in Starshield services for Ukraine, a US official said on Friday, after tech billionaire Elon Musk insisted any limits on the communications system would ultimately have come from the president.

Kyiv on Wednesday reported restrictions to the SpaceX-operated service, which it sees as crucial to fending off Moscow’s invasion, shortly after Trump criticised Ukraine and urged it to stop targeting Russian oil refineries.

“No such request was ever made by the president,” the US official said when asked whether the order had come from the White House.

Musk has said that “any limits on speed or usage” of his SpaceX company’s Starshield systems were “decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS”, referring to Trump.

Ukraine uses Starshield, Starlink’s military-grade satellite service, for its battlefield communications, its mid-range strikes on Russia-occupied territory, and its interceptor drones.

It also uses SpaceX’s parallel Starlink civilian satellite system.

Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Friday that the service was in the process of being restored, and that “my partners told me that the administration and the White House sent a message to SpaceX asking them” to do so.

Relations between Washington and Kyiv have been increasingly tense in recent days, with Trump calling for Zelensky to be replaced after the Ukrainian leader slammed a US deal allowing more Russian diesel into global markets.

title: From hospital, Pope pushes Putin for ceasefire in Ukraine city
text:
VATICAN CITY: Pope Leo XIV spoke with Russian President Vladimir Putin by phone on Friday, calling for a ceasefire in a Russian-occupied city in southern Ukraine, as he recovers in hospital from alung canceroperation.

The Vatican said that Pope Leo “expressed his deep concern about the grave humanitarian situation in the city of Oleshky, in the Kherson region, and called for a ceasefire to allow the delivery of food and medical assistance, and the voluntary and safe evacuation of the civilian population”.

The surprise notice from the Vatican on Friday evening suggested that the recovering pope is still hard at work, despite this week’s operation to remove a cancerous tumour from his right lung.

Residents of Oleshky, in southern Ukraine, are facing a worsening humanitarian crisis with shortages of food and medication as they are caught in the crossfire between Russian and Ukrainian troops.

The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Turk, denounced a “desperate” situation in the city, calling on Russia to enable civilians to evacuate.

In a note, the Kremlin said the two had talked and “a detailed explanation was provided regarding the Kyiv regime’s responsibility for the difficult humanitarian situation” in Oleshky.

The Kremlin said Putin also wished the pope a speedy recovery and stressed the “importance of Russian-Vatican cooperation in promoting unifying spiritual and moral values”.

Earlier in the day, the pontiff celebrated mass on the top floor of Rome’s Gemelli hospital, as seen in the first images of him released by the Vatican since the procedure.

The images showed the 71-year-old Chicago-born pope in front of a makeshift altar in a room on the 10th floor, dressed in a green vestment.

He appeared relaxed and in good form in the two photos released, standing with his private secretary, Peruvian priest Edgard Rimaycuna, at his side.

title: Why India’s voter revision drive has stoked fear and anger
text:
NEW DELHI: India’s sweeping overhaul of electoral rolls has triggered a political firestorm, with opposition parties accusing the election commission of putting millions at risk of disenfranchisement.

The Special Intensive Revision (SIR), launched in June last year, aims to purge electoral rolls of “duplicate, deceased and otherwise ineligible” voters.

Critics, however, say the exercise has shifted the burden of proof onto voters, forcing millions to establish their eligibility and raising the risk of wrongful exclusion.

Thousands have held protests in the capital this month calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner over accusations that the rolls have been manipulated to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party.

The Election Commission of India (ECI) rejects the allegations, saying the revision complies with the law and that omission from a draft roll does not amount to permanent deletion.

Nearly 650 million of the 960m registered voters cast their ballot in the last general election in 2024.

Election rolls are routinely updated to reflect deaths, address changes and newly eligible voters.

But the SIR goes much further, requiring the entire electorate to re-establish their credentials by filling out extra forms and providing documentation linking them to old electoral rolls.

“This procedure is entirely different from what has been done in the past,” former election commissioner Ashok Lavasa said.

“The methodology followed has been of physical door-to-door verification. It was never that you asked people wholesale to establish their eligibility all over again even after they have been admitted to the rolls through the prescribed due process.”

Transparency activist Anjali Bhardwaj said the process disproportionately burdens marginalised voters who often struggle to produce documents.

“The crisis of documents is the biggest crisis the poor face in most cases,” she said.

“Women, minorities, people living at the margins and the poorest were the worst hit by this exercise because they’re the ones who find it very difficult to produce documents which can prove their citizenship.”

More than 133m names were excluded from revised electoral rolls, according to figures reported by Indian media and cited by opposition parties in court filings.

The ECI disputes the characterisation of those cases as confirmed deletions, saying eligible voters remain entitled to apply for inclusion on the roll.

According to an ECI breakdown, around 28m entries were classified as belonging to deceased voters and 10.4m as duplicates, while millions of others were marked as absent, shifted or untraceable.

The data does not specify how many voters were ultimately found to be ineligible.

“If the intention was to remove ineligible people, then they must say how many ineligible people were found,” Lavasa said.

title: Zelensky smiles on being asked whether Trump  is scapegoating him
text:
BRUSSELS: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zele­­nsky gave a knowing smile and stayed mum on Friday when asked if the US president was scapegoating him for troubles in the US.

“This is my answer,” Zelensky said, as journalists broke into laughter at a press conference in Brussels after he met EU leaders.

Zelensky had been asked if Donald Trump was lashing out at the Ukrainian leader as a way to deflect from his own political strife ahead of next month’s midterm elections as he is bogged down with Iran and diesel prices have soared.

The question came after Trump said he found it easier to deal with Russian President Vla­dimir Putin than Zelensky as ties have soured with Kyiv.

“Yesterday was a thousand drones in Ukraine, a thousand, but the American side said that it is difficult to speak with Zelensky, it’s less difficult to manage with Putin,” Zelensky said.

title: Red Cross ambulance driver shot dead in Ethiopia
text:
GENEVA: A Red Cross ambulance driver was shot dead in Ethiopia while on duty transporting a patient, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies said on Friday.

Mulugeta Andualem was killed in the Benishangul-Gumuz region of western Ethiopia on Wednesday.

The Ethiopian Red Cross Society ambulance driver was hit when armed individuals opened fire on the vehicle in a remote, high-risk area about 50 kilometres from the town of Woreda.

Since the conflict in Sudan began in April 2023, a total of 25 Red Cross volunteers have been killed.

Benishangul-Gumuz is home to armed groups, some of which have joined the Ethiopian Peoples Forces Alliance for Survival, which brings together the main anti-government armed groups from across the vast, multi-ethnic country.

“No one should lose their life while providing medical assistance,” the Geneva-based IFRC said in a statement.

“Humanitarian personnel, ambulances, and medical facilities must be protected. Health teams must be able to reach people in need without fear of being attacked or losing their lives.”

title: Four killed battling fires in Indonesia as toxic haze cloaks region
text:
JAKARTA: Four people died on Indonesia’s Java island fighting the blazes that have sent toxic smoke across southeast Asia, closed schools and fuelled a surge of respiratory complaints, authorities said on Friday.

The four lost their lives in East Java’s Bromo Tengger Semeru National Park.

Two others suffered serious burns and were receiving further medical treatment.

“This incident serves as a reminder that forest and land fire extinguishing is a high-risk operation,” it said, adding that personnel safety remained a primary concern.

Singapore to take action against 7 Indonesian firms for ‘causing or contributing’ to haze

The impact of the months-long fires has also prompted Singapore’s leader to vow legal action against any companies responsible for the blazes that have made regional air quality among the world’s worst.

Singapore again topped IQAir’s live ranking of the world’s most polluted major cities on Friday, with Kuala Lumpur second and Jakarta eighth.

“Where warranted, we will take action under Singapore’s Transboundary Haze Pollution Act, and also explore joint action with other countries,” said Prime Minister Lawrence Wong.

Authorities said Singapore had put on notice seven Indonesian firms whose “activities caused or contributed to unhealthy haze levels”.

Legal experts have cautioned that pursuing companies linked to the smoke is challenging, with investigations reliant on cooperation from foreign authorities.

Singapore has no plantations or forests of its own, but several companies with concessions in Indonesia are reportedly based in the city state.

Indonesia’s forestry department said there was a significant jump in hotspots in several areas in six “priority provinces” where 615 hotspots were detected.

A hotspot is a location where a satellite detects an unusually high temperature, indicating a potential fire or other strong heat source.

Singapore’s investigations into four Indonesian companies over their alleged role in the 2015 haze crisis remain open, a case that strained relations with Jakarta at the time.

An official at Indonesia’s national police investigations agency on Wednesday said it was probing companies responsible for the fires, but did not give specific names.

Indonesia experiences wildfires regularly during its dry season, but this year the blazes have been especially severe because a strong El Nino has brought drought.

While drought contributes to the fires, experts say deforestation and drying of peatlands has damaged previously fire-resistant landscapes.

“We cannot control the weather or the winds, nor can we directly control what happens beyond our borders,” said Singapore leader Wong.

“But we will do everything we can to protect Singaporeans, while working with our neighbours to address the underlying causes of the haze.”
