title: Strengthening LGs
text:
THE ECP has done well to refuse to allow the Punjab administration to push the local government elections to April. It should now hold its ground. Four years after the last elected councils left office, the province is still looking for reasons not to hold the polls. The reasons, though, keep changing. In August, the provincial authorities agreed to a window between Dec 15 and Jan 15. Two months later, they discovered that the months of December and January are foggy and cold, and that Ramazan would begin in February. None of this is news. Winter arrives every year, and the Ramazan calendar was not a surprise to anyone who signed off on the August consultations. LGs are the tier of the state closest to the people. They handle sanitation, water supply, street lighting, primary health and schooling, and local roads, and generally keep the town running. In functioning democracies, this is where citizens learn to hold someone accountable, and where future political leaders learn to govern. Provincial and federal parties know this, and many are uncomfortable with the fact. An elected mayor with a budget and a mandate is a rival centre of power. A commissioner or deputy commissioner who answers to the chief minister is not. So elections are delayed, laws rewritten whenever the government changes, and administrators fill the space that elected representatives should occupy.

The Constitution requires each province to set up an LG system and devolve political, administrative and financial responsibility, and authority to its elected representatives. Holding elections is only the first step. Every provincial government, especially Punjab, has treated even that step as optional, and the ones that have held elections have often hollowed out the institutions afterwards. Councils without control over their own funds, staff or functions are decorative. This matters more now than it did before. The debate on improving governance by creating new provinces has gathered pace, and it rests on a sound observation. Provinces are too centralised to serve their citizens from afar. A new provincial map, however, will not help. The new provinces will continue to behave like the old ones, hoarding power and funds at the top. If the aim is better governance, the more direct route is to strengthen the tier that already exists in the Constitution but has never been allowed to work.

title: No talks
text:
THE opposition Tehreek-i-Tahafuz Ayin-i-Pakistan hasannouncedthat there will be no more talks with the government till the latter yields on the one thing it has resolutely sought to prevent: a meeting with jailed former prime minister Imran Khan. Having handed authority for further negotiation to Leader of the Opposition in the National Assembly Mahmood Khan Achakzai, the TTAP has made that meeting a precondition for a return to the table.

If there is any desire among the decision-makers to keep political temperatures in check, the government will take up Mr Achakzai’s offer to reason with Imran. The opposition leader is, after all, a veteran politician viewed with respect across party lines. Unfortunately, it is unlikely that the government is in a reflective mood. It not only managed to dismiss the elected PTI government in KP, but has also had its decision approved by a joint sitting of parliament.

That move has poisoned the well. The trouble is that few, other than those who imposed emergency andgovernor’s rule on KP, are convinced of the government’s ‘security’ rationale, which they see as a fig leaf for an overreaction by the government and its allies, that is unlikely to hold for long: the set-up imposed on the province faces daunting odds.

In the four-and-a-half years since the PTI’s government in the centre was ousted, its successors have failed to deliver better living conditions to the people. The people have only heard the words ‘austerity’ and ‘stabilisation’ during this period, and it has often seemed that the former, in particular, has applied only to the public at large, while those responsible for steering the country out of a protracted polycrisis have merely assigned blame and levelled accusations. Every day that passes adds to the public’s disaffection with the mode of governance.

The government should understand that the PTI’s protest march and its reaction to it will look like nothing more than a storm in a teacup on the timescale against which governance is measured. It may not realise it, but it has fallen into the same trap the PTI fell into during its truncated time in power.

The PTI remained obsessed with hounding its opponents over corruption; the governments that have followed it have similarly consumed themselves with hounding the PTI out of the political sphere. All seem to be missing the big picture — an economy stretched to its limits and a populace experiencing increasing levels of hunger and poverty while outsized egos clash against each other.

It is regrettable that the politics of one of the largest, most populous nations of the world has been reduced to single-item vendettas. This must stop. Mr Achakzai has offered a way back to the table, and the government should seize the opportunity.

title: Stocks post marginal gains as volatility persists
text:
KARACHI: Despite persistent volatility, the Pakistan Stock Exchange (PSX) closed higher on Friday for the third consecutive session, keeping the benchmark index in positive territory. However, regional and political turmoil continued to weigh on investor sentiment, while the economic outlook remained uncertain.

Topline Securities Ltd said the market traded range-bound, with the index moving both ways before closing at 166,419.72, up 233.55 points or 0.14 per cent. This was attributed to a lack of triggers and elevated crude oil prices.

Systems Ltd, United Bank, MCB Bank, Bank Al-Habib, and Engro Fertiliser collectively contributed 269 points to the index. Conversely, Oil and Gas Development Compa­­ny, Lucky Cement, Mee­zan Bank, Pakistan Te­­le­communication Company, and Engro Holdings wiped out 223 points.

Ali Najib, Deputy Head of Trading at Arif Habib Ltd, said the PSX remained volatile, moving in both directions amid cautious investor sentiment, driven by geopolitical uncertainty and position-squaring ahead of the weekend.

The index staged a partial recovery, touching an intraday high of 166,708 before giving up some of its gains.

On the macroeconomic front, Pakistan recorded a current account deficit of $356m in September, compared with a surplus of $133m in September 2025 and a deficit of $73m in August.

This pushed the 1QFY27 deficit to $874m, up from $755m in the same period last year. Meanwhile, the Real Effective Exchange Rate rose to 108.93 in September from 107.87 in August, marking its highest level since May 2018.

On the corporate front, UBL reported a profit after tax of Rs30.6bn in 3QCY26 (earnings per share of Rs12.24), down 13pc year on year and 18pc quarter on quarter. However, 9MCY26 earnings rose 16pc year on year to Rs117bn (EPS: Rs46.5). The bank announced a quarterly dividend of Rs8 per share, taking its cumulative 9MCY26 payout to Rs24 per share.

Market participation weakened sharply, reflecting investor caution, as trading volume fell well below the 500-million mark, tumbling 23.31pc to 396.9 million shares. Total turnover dipped 20.75pc to Rs18.6bn. Pakistan Refinery topped the volume chart with 38.4 million shares.

Analysts expect the market to remain volatile and range-bound between 164,000 and 168,000 amid cautious investor sentiment and evolving macroeconomic and geopolitical developments.

title: Oil rebounds 3pc
text:
HOUSTON: Oil prices gained more than 3 per cent and were heading for weekly gains on continued uncertainty over Middle East supplies, and as investors kept assessing how much diesel Russia could supply to the global markets.

Brent crude futures were up $3.41, or 3.2pc, at $109.34 at 12:41pm ET (1641 GMT), while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures rose $2.74, or 2.8pc, to $100.67, crossing $100 for the first time since Sept 21.

So far this week, Brent has risen 4.1pc and WTI 8.6pc.

“Conflict in the Middle East still keeps coming back and I think it’s questionable how much diesel fuel Russia can actually deliver to the markets. Those two factors are just continuing to have traders be buyers,” said Dennis Kissler, senior vice president of trading at BOK Financial.

Supply concerns also increased as attacks around the Strait of Hormuz surged over the past 10 days.

title: Big industry output posts meagre rise
text:
ISLAMABAD: Large-Scale Manufacturing (LSM) posted a paltry 0.67 per cent growth in August, signalling a slowdown in the industrial sector.

The Quantum Index of Manufacturing stood at 113.19 in August, up from 112.45 in the corresponding month of the last year. On a month-on-month basis, production fell by 4.96pc in August from July, the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics said on Friday.

In the first two months (July-August) of 2026-27, the LSM grew modestly by 1.85pc YoY. Industrial activity rebounded 3.03pc in July after production contracted sharply by 3.48pc in June.

In FY26, LSM sector output expanded 4.98pc on YoY basis, suggesting industrial production regained some ground.

The main contributors to overall growth in 2MFY27 were tobacco (0.37 percentage points), wearing apparel (2.85), petroleum products (1.17), cement (0.07), electrical equipment (0.13pc), automobiles (1.20), other transport equipment (0.27), and furniture (0.43).

However, the recovery was uneven, with food dragging LSM growth by 1.20 percentage points, beverages (-0.37), textiles (-0.52), chemicals (-0.89), pharmaceuticals (-0.86), iron & steel products (-0.48), machinery and equipment (-0.01).

The weakness in textiles is particularly significant given the sector’s weight in Pakistan’s manufacturing and export base, suggesting that the improvement in headline LSM growth did not extend evenly across some of the country’s major industrial activities.

Negative contributions from textiles, pharmaceuticals, chemicals, and iron and steel suggest that while industrial production recovered in July as a whole, momentum remained fragile and concentrated in a relatively small group of industries.

The food group dipped 8.86pc in July-August YoY. Wheat and rice milling declined 3.38pc. The cooking oil production decreased 20.46pc, vegetable ghee production fell 16.57pc.  However, tea blended posted a negative growth of 2.84pc.

The overall textile sector partly posted a negative growth of 2.98pc in 2MFY27 on a YoY basis. Cotton yarn rose 2.09pc, while cotton cloth fell 0.03pc, accounting for more than 80pc of the textile sector. Garment exports grew 16.69pc.

Coke and petroleum products surged 15.48pc in 2MFY27. Most petroleum products posted positive production growth during the months under review. Petrol production rose by 24.69pc, while high-speed diesel rose by 10.10pc. LPG production rose by 17.65pc, and kerosene by 28.10pc during the months under review. However, furnace oil output dipped by 44.37pc.

The automobile sector grew 32.45pc in 2MFY27 YoY. This growth was mainly driven by a 30.45pc rise in jeeps and cars, followed by trucks at 77.70pc and buses at 13.91pc. However, LCV production declined 15.99pc.

Pharmaceutical production dipped 14.57pc, and fertiliser production fell 7.55pc. Iron and steel production declined 11.48pc in 2MFY27. The production of rubber products surged by 2.50pc, non-metallic minerals by 0.20pc and electrical equipment by 4.99pc.

title: CAD swells to $874m in July-Sept
text:
KARACHI: The current account posted a deficit of more than $874 million in the first quarter of the current fiscal year, mainly due to a widening trade gap.

State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) data on Friday showed the current account deficit (CAD) swelled to $874m in July-September, up from $755m in the same period last year.

The deterioration was particularly pronounced in September, when the current account recorded a deficit of $356m compared to a surplus of $133m in the same month last year.

The first-quarter deficit has already exceeded the $391m CAD recorded for the entire FY26.

During July-September FY27, the country’s trade deficit increased by more than 15 per cent to $10.79bn from $9.37bn in the corresponding period last year.

Foreign direct investment increases 20pc to $719.7m in first quarter

The widening trade gap reflects not only higher international oil and gas prices but also a rising food import bill. After cotton, Pakistan has also been importing wheat, while edible oil imports remained a major burden as they reached $3.357bn in FY26.

The total food import bill stood at $8.3bn in FY26, while petroleum imports amounted to $15.5bn.

The rising import bill has increased pressure on the current account despite remittance inflows of more than $41bn in FY26.

Goods exports during July-September FY27 rose by $604m to $8.454bn from $7.853bn a year earlier. However, imports increased by more than $2.2bn to $17.784bn from $15.558bn during the same period last year.

Both exports and imports of services also increased by almost half a billion dollars during the first quarter.

The faster rise in imports relative to exports suggests that the current account deficit could widen further during FY27 unless the trade imbalance eases.

Financial experts believe the CAD could increase further if the conflict in the Gulf persists and international oil prices remain elevated.

Meanwhile, foreign direct investment (FDI) increased by 20pc during the first quarter of FY27 despite regional and domestic uncertainty.

SBP data showed FDI reached $719.7m during July-September FY27 compared to $600.4m in the corresponding period of last fiscal year, showing an increase of $119.3m.

While the inflow remains modest relative to the size of Pakistan’s economy, the year-on-year increase could support stronger investment flows during the remaining nine months of the fiscal year.

FDI in September alone rose to $219.5m from $185.3m in the same month last year, an increase of about $34m.

China has traditionally been Pakistan’s largest source of foreign investment, but Canada emerged as the biggest investor during the first quarter, with inflows of $229m compared to $225m a year earlier.

FDI from China increased to $197.5m from $121m during the same period last year.

Other major inflows included $83.4m from the United Kingdom, $54.8m from the United Arab Emirates and $25.6m from Hong Kong.

title: Joint sitting gives blessing to emergency, governor’s rule
text:
• Centre insists security situation in KP left it with ‘no other option’• PTI rejects govt claim it ‘backed terrorists’, terms federal measures ‘unconstitutional’• Naqvi claims talks continued until last possible moment• JUI-F says no evidence presented to justify governor’s rule

ISLAMABAD: A joint sitting of parliament on Thu­rsday approved the federal government’s imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakh­tunkhwa amid a strong protest from the opposition.

The session had been summoned to consider separate resolutions on the two measures imposed in the PTI-ruled province on Oct 11, as the government cited the provincial administration’s alleged “deliberate disengagement” from the fight against terrorism.

The move followed weeks of tensions between the Centre and PTI, as well as negotiations aimed at bridging differences, after the opposition party announced a protest march seeking the release of its jailed founder, Imran Khan.

Opposition members attended the joint sitting carrying placards bearing slogans such as “emergency na manzoor” (emergency is unacceptable). Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif attended part of the proceedings and shook hands with opposition leaders in both houses.

Parliamentary Affairs Minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry tabled the proclamations and resolutions relating to the emergency and governor’s rule.

Earlier, he moved a motion under Rule 232 of the Parliament (Joint Sitting) Rules, 1973, to suspend certain sub-rules to allow the resolutions to be moved. Amid loud opposition protests, the motion was adopted by 214 votes to 56.

Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar, opening the debate, said treasury members were ready to respond to any questions raised by the opposition and explained the constitutional procedure for approval of the proclamations.

After hours of debate, National Assembly Spea­ker Ayaz Sadiq put the two resolutions to a vote as opposition members continued chanting against the emergency. Both resolutions were passed.

The joint sitting came a day after both houses of parliament separately endorsed the proclamation of emergency.

Under Article 232 of the Constitution, if the president issues a proclamation of emergency on his own, it must be placed before both houses for approval within 10 days.

A proclamation of governor’s rule under Article 234 must be placed before a joint sitting and ceases to operate after two months unless extended by parliament. It cannot remain in force for more than six months.

Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi said the federal government had been left with “no option” but to impose emergency and governor’s rule and insisted that it had tried until the last moment to avoid such a step.

“By God, our hearts did not want to do this,” he said, urging the opposition not to accuse the government of exploiting terrorism for political purposes.

Mr Naqvi rejected PTI’s claim that the government delegation had walked out of negotiations, stressing that the Centre remained engaged until the end.

He said the government had proposed declaring an emergency in 12 districts of KP and claimed PTI leader Asad Qaiser had initially been willing to sign an agreement, but was advised to consult the provincial government.

The interior minister acknowledged that PTI representatives involved in the talks had taken a clear position against terrorism, but said the Centre and province could not pursue “two different policies” on the issue.

He criticised Chief Minister Sohail Afridi, whose role became non-functional after the imposition of governor’s rule, for insufficient engagement with counterterrorism efforts.

He claimed that Mr Afridi had not gone to the site of “even a single operation with the army and only used to say, ‘I cannot afford this politically’”.

Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar later defended the measures as a “difficult decision” taken in accordance with the Constitution.

He recalled previous counterterrorism operations and the National Action Plan adopted after the 2014 Army Public School attack, arguing that terrorism had to be addressed before political differences.

Mr Dar alleged that certain individuals within PTI had contributed to policies that allowed terrorists to regain space, while stressing that he did not regard the party as a whole as supportive of terrorism.

He also criticised Mr Afridi for political mobilisation while KP faced a worsening security situation, insisting that governance in the province had “collapsed”.

PTI interim chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan strongly rejected allegations that the provincial government had supported terrorists and sought an apology from the prime minister.

“The prime minister has alleged that we are supporting terrorists. We are disappointed to hear that. You have to apologise to the entire population of KP and us,” he said.

He warned that portraying a federating unit as supporting terrorism could have serious implications for Pakistan internationally.

Barrister Gohar reje­cted both the emergency and governor’s rule as unconstitutional and said PTI would challenge the measures at every available forum.

He also disputed government claims that PTI had caused the breakdown of talks and urged the Centre not to politicise terrorism.

National Assembly Opposition Leader Mehmood Khan Achakzai also opposed the measures and blamed “faulty decisions” by successive rulers for the current security situation.

He said the opposition was ready for dialogue on strengthening parliament and eliminating terrorism, and sought meetings between Imran Khan and his family, friends and party workers.

Senate Opposition Leader Allama Raja Nasir Abbas also accused the government delegation of derailing negotiations and said more time should have been allowed for dialogue.

PPP Vice President Sherry Rehman disputed PTI’s account of the Oct 3 talks, insisting that the government delegation had remained at the negotiating table and was prepared to continue discussions late into the night.

She said President Asif Ali Zardari and PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari had consistently favoured dialogue, while stressing that terrorism remained a “red line” for the party.

However, she said the PPP would not support any emergency that violated the Constitution.

“If you think PPP is going to support any sort of emergency which is against the Constitution, you are wrong,” she said.

JUI-F Senator Kamran Murtaza, who had earlier submitted a resolution opposing governor’s rule, argued that parliament had not been provided documentary evidence justifying the decision.

He said a proclamation under Article 234 required a report from the KP governor and contended that no such report explaining the necessity for governor’s rule had been presented before parliament.

title: Riyadh points the finger at Iran amid fresh Houthi salvos
text:
• Saudi official accuses Iran of encouraging latest escalation; coalition spox claims ‘regional actors’ supplied rebels with advanced weapons• Cabinet members ‘safe’ after missile strike on Aden’s presidential palace leaves four dead• Pakistan condemns attacks against civilian, economic infrastructure; rebels deny targeting Madina

RIYADH: The Saudi-led military coalition fighting in Yemen accused regional actors on Thursday of helping the Houthis acquire advanced military technologies, while Riyadh pointed the finger at Tehran for encouraging an escalation in the long-running conflict.

The accusations came as the Houthis fired missiles at the presidential palace complex in Yemen’s southern city of Aden on Thursday, killing at least four people, while the coalition detailed dozens of cross-border strikes on Saudi infrastructure.

During a briefing in Riyadh, coalition spokesperson Turki al-Malki said the Houthis had worked with unidentified regional actors to obtain advanced weaponry, including ballistic missiles, attack and suicide drones, and fast explosive-laden boats.

While al-Malki did not name the countries involved, Saudi Arabia’s deputy minister for public diplomacy at the foreign ministry pointed the finger directly at Tehran during a separate virtual briefing with reporters.

“Iran continues to arm, train and support the Houthis in violation of UN Security Council resolutions,” Dr Rayed Krimly said. “We think that the escalation by the Houthis at this latest stage of the conflict is encouraged by Iran.”

“Overall, it doesn’t seem yet that the Iranians are able to provide the necessary concessions for a solution,” Krimly said.

He also accused the Houthis of refusing to attend peace talks in Oman as fighting ramped up.

“At the beginning of this escalation, we asked them to meet in Mus­cat, Oman, and they refused,” he added. “This was the last communication which happened a few weeks ago.”

On the ground in Yemen, Houthi forces struck the Al-Maashiq presidential palace in Aden, the seat of Yemen’s Saudi-backed and internationally recognised government.

It was the first attack on the complex since Yemen’s civil war flared back to life in July following the collapse of a 2022 UN-brokered truce.

Yemeni government sources said at least four people were killed and 10 wounded in the strikes, while officials told Reuters that two guards were among the dead. Witnesses reported hearing loud booms and seeing smoke rise from the site.

Yemeni Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani said the prime minister and cabinet members were safe following the attack, which involved five missiles and drones.

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group had bom­bed what he described as a Saudi military operations headquarters and weapons depots run by Saudi officers inside the palace complex, calling it part of a policy of targeting “Saudi reinforcements wherever they were located”.

Yemeni government forces added that the Houthis also fired several ballistic missiles at the central oil-rich city of Marib on Thursday, while residents in Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city, reported intensifying bombardment and dwindling supplies.

Al-Malki told reporters the Houthis had launched 20 attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh in October alone, killing 17 people and wounding 333 others.

“The Houthis must immediately cease all terrorist operations targeting civilians and civilian facilities, including airports, ports, oil facilities, and infrastructure,” al-Malki said.

Earlier on Thursday, the coalition said it intercepted and destroyed Houthi drones launched toward Saudi Arabia’s southern region and the southwestern city of Khamis Mushait, after civil defence authorities issued a brief early-warning alert in the southern province of Najran.

Al-Malki also announced on the social platform X that coalition forces had achieved the “interception and destruction of a cruise missile in the Madina region”.

The Houthis quickly denied targeting the region, but Saree warned airlines that Saudi airspace and airports were unsafe.

“The Yemeni armed forces confirm that they have not carried out any operation today targeting Saudi territory, and that the Saudi enemy’s claims of an attack on Madina are a shameless and brazen lie,” he wrote on X.

At the United Nations on Thursday, Pakistan strongly condemned the Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia’s civilian and economic infrastructure.

Speaking at a UN Security Council debate on the Middle East, Ambassador Usman Jadoon demanded an immediate end to the strikes and backed the UN special envoy’s efforts to resume dialogue in Yemen.

“We reiterate our unwavering support for the security, sovereignty and territorial integrity of the brotherly Kingdom, and reaffirm its right to self-defence under international law against any external attacks,” Jadoon said.

France’s ambassador, Jérôme Bonnafont, also cited Tehran’s support for the Houthis as a destabilising regional activity during the debate and reaffirmed solidarity with Saudi and Yemeni authorities as the council considered a presidential statement on the escalation.

title: Rain in Lahore

LAHORE: Rain hit several cities across Punjab over the 24-hour period.

According to the Provincial Disaster Management Authority (PDMA) data, Noorpur Thal received maximum rainfall of 48 millimetres, followed by Sargodha with 32mm.

title: Bullet-riddled body of teacher found in Pasni
text:
GWADAR: The bullet-riddled body of a schoolteacher was found in the Pasni area of Gwadar district on Thursday.

According to police, the people of Pasni informed the administration about the presence of a body in the area. Police rushed to the area and shifted the body to the district hospital.

The body was identified as that of schoolteacher Pervez Ahmed, who had gone missing two days ago. His family members tried to find him, but he was not traced.

The deceased was an Arabic language teacher at a government high school.

The family said Pervez Ahmed was abducted from Pasni bazaar by unidentified individuals two days ago and now his body was found in the outskirts of Pasni town.

title: A chatbot to plug e-governance information gaps
text:
LAHORE: Getting access to government services can prove costly, time-consuming and confusing.

Though a myriad of services are provided through free government-run e-platforms, these remain fragmented across various domains, forcing people to run from pillar to post just to ascertain how they should go about availing a specific service.

To solve this problem, a Karachi-based developer has come up with a simple yet elegant solution.

The ‘Ask Pakistan’ platform, the brainchild of Raheel Siddiqui, is a website where a chatbot can help people seeking government services obtain the required information, thus bridging the gap between the state and its citizens.

Talking toDawn, Mr Siddiqui said that many non-tech-savvy people struggled with getting the required information.

Raheel Siddiqui’s ‘Ask Pakistan’ platform aims to help the less tech-savvy easily access govt services

“The information is available and the government is actually good in providing directions on how to avail public services, but the problem is that there are a lot of services. There is no unified platform which can give you information about all of them.” This, he said, was his motivation behind building the platform.

The idea came to him when his friend saw a tweet about a US government website that collated all citizen-related services on one page. “He said that it will be great if we have something like this in Pakistan. It took me a couple of hours to build the basic app and I sent it to him. He used it and told me to post about it online, and I did.”

Mr Siddiqui didn’t expect a lot of attention and said that he was surprised when it went viral. “I got something like 500,000 views in a few hours,” he added.

He described his platform as an information provider and said that it only provided publicly available data, which was already there but was scattered across different government bodies on a large number of separate websites.

The pakistangov.online website has a simple interface with bilingual labels for each section, and it greets the user with the message: “Ask anything about a government service. Get a clear answer from official sources, with the next steps.” The website has no sign-up, and it doesn’t require users to input any personal information. According to Mr Siddiqui, privacy was always a concern, which is reflected in how the website is set up.

Users can input their queries, with common questions such as “How do I renew my CNIC?” being offered as examples. The questions can be in English, Urdu or Roman Urdu. After processing the query, the chatbot gives a detailed step-by-step answer.

The platform currently collates information from 52 government websites, including the Directorate General of Immigration & Passports, National Database & Registration Authority (Nadra), Federal Board of Revenue (FBR), Benazir Income Support Programme (BISP), Higher Education Commission (HEC), as well as many other federal and provincial departments.

For ease of use, users can also browse by topic, and the website also links directly to the most commonly used government departments.

Giving an example of availing a government-provided public service, he said that if you want to get a passport, you have to go to the passport office early in the morning, get in line and pay a broker to get a passport.

“But if you have a platform where you can get an appointment, after a verification process, you won’t have to go through all this hassle,” he explained, and said that another thing that could happen was that, after filling out the required information through an app at home, the citizen could get their passport without even visiting the office.

He said, “This is being done for getting a CNIC and it can also be done for a passport or any other service. Pakistan has the PakID app, which is very good and a lot of services are being offered on it but people don’t know about it.”

While internet services are available in villages across the country, there is a lack of awareness about the e-services being provided by the government. “My app focuses on solving this information gap problem. All you have to do is give it a prompt and it can guide you about the required service,” he said.

On X (formerly Twitter), many first-time users described their experience of using the ‘Ask Pakistan’ chatbot and praised Mr Siddiqui’s initiative.

“Simple and elegant UI makes UX a breeze of fresh air and all the useful links are a cherry on the top,” wrote Muhammad Ishfaque.

Another user, Wasey Azim, wrote that he had asked the chatbot a question about Pakistani visas. “It gave an answer no other service could provide,” he said.

Usman Shabbir also posted a query about the visa requirements for his US-born son to travel to Pakistan. “I struggled with this question for hours last time I travelled from NYC to Pakistan,” he posted on X, and indicated that he found the answer quite easily thanks to ‘Ask Pakistan’.

Many users also called for official integration, with Raja Mannan Khan saying that he was “waiting for agentic AI integration” of the chatbot.

Mr Siddiqui toldDawnthat he was surprised when the government showed an interest in his work. Being Gen Z, he said he used to think of the government as a ‘very old-school and laid-back organisation’.

“Recently, the IT minister also contacted me and I am talking to the ministry’s team about the future direction of the project. They are very open and I think they have some great ideas and need people to execute these ideas. They have been very good and supportive and asked me what I needed to further this platform,” he said, adding that he was very surprised by it.

However, he said that a platform that not only guides but also provides online e-governance services could only be developed and controlled by the government itself.

When contacted, Federal Minister for Information Technology (MoIT) Shaza Fatima Khawaja confirmed the ministry’s interest in the project and said that Mr Siddiqui had been invited to the ministry in Islamabad. Subsequently, Mr Siddiqui presented his work to the minister and her team at the MoIT.

title: ATC directs jail trial in security breach case against Imaan, Hadi
text:
ISLAMABAD: An anti-terrorism court on Thursday directed lawyers and witnesses in a case against incarcerated rights activist and lawyer Imaan Zainab Mazari-Hazir and her husband, Hadi Ali Chattha, to appear at Adiala jail today (Friday) for the next hearing after police cited difficulties in transporting the accused to court.

The court also directed the Adiala jail superintendent to arrange a meeting between Ms Imaan and her counsel, after the defence submitted an affidavit detailing alleged difficulties during a previous meeting.

ATC Judge Tahir Abbas Sipra was hearing a case concerning the alleged disruption of a security route for an international cricket team and incitement to public unrest. The couple have been accused of removing barriers from the route and were indicted on Oct 7.

Defence lawyer Aimal Khan Mandokhail submitted an affidavit stating that he had presented the court’s order to the jail deputy superintendent and sought a private meeting with his client.

Police tell judge they lack vehicles, personnel to bring couple to court

According to the affidavit, the accused said they were not boycotting the trial and wanted to appear in person, citing audio and internet problems during video-link proceedings that hindered their ability to follow hearings and consult their lawyers.

The court was informed that jail authorities had requested a vehicle to transport the couple, but Islamabad police had said they lacked the required vehicle and three constables to accompany them.

Superintendent of Police (Headquarters) Pari Gul told the court that a large police contingent was deployed in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and suggested holding the trial on jail premises.

Expressing dismay, Judge Sipra said he had repeatedly directed that the accused be produced in court and questioned why police had not made the request earlier. He said their “actions have completely altered the course of the matter”.

Ms Imaan’s mother, former human rights minister Shireen Mazari, asked how her daughter and son-in-law had previously been brought to court at 10pm, accompanied by 12 vehicles.

Ms Imaan and Mr Chattha subsequently appeared via video link, and the judge briefed them on the proceedings. Ms Gul said a formal notification regarding the jail trial would be issued the same day.

Mr Chattha said he had no objection to appearing in person or undergoing a jail trial, but stressed that lawyers and journalists should also be allowed to attend proceedings at the jail.

title: No compromise on law and order: Ziaullah Langove
text:
QUETTA: Balochistan Home Minister Ziaullah Langove said on Thursday that there would be no compromise on maintaining peace and order and ensuring security in the province.

Presiding over a meeting to review the law and order situation in Qila Abdullah district, Mr Langove said the provincial government was taking all possible steps to fulfil its basic responsibilities, including maintaining law and order, combating drug abuse and trafficking, and protecting citizens’ lives and property.

A day earlier, opposition and treasury members had expressed concern over the deteriorating law and order situation in Qila Abdullah, a district bordering Afghanistan, during a session of the Balochistan Assembly.

The meeting was attended by MPA Engineer Zamarak Khan Achakzai, Additional Home Secretary Hamza Shafqaat, the inspector general of prisons, the Qila Abdullah deputy commissioner, Pishin District Police Officer Khalil Bugti and other relevant officials.

Minister vows action against kidnappers, drug traffickers in Qila Abdullah

Participants reviewed the overall law and order situation in Qila Abdullah. Relevant officials briefed the meeting on security measures being implemented in the area and the challenges they faced.

“Protecting citizens’ lives and property is the government’s top priority,” Mr Langove said, adding that further measures were being taken against those involved in kidnapping, drug trafficking and other illegal activities threatening law and order in the area.

He said security forces were also conducting intelligence-based operations (IBOs) against terrorists in Qila Abdullah and other parts of the province to provide a peaceful environment for residents.

He directed the relevant authorities to take effective measures to improve law and order, prevent crime and eliminate drugs, emphasising that these efforts were essential to ensuring a safe and secure environment for citizens.

title: IHC seeks PTI response in case about Imran’s X account
text:
ISLAMABAD: The Isla­mabad High Court (IHC) on Thursday granted PTI interim chairman Barris­ter Gohar Ali Khan additional time to submit a written response to a petition seeking a ban on party founder Imran Khan’s official X account, adjourning the hearing until Nov 23.

Justice Arbab Muham­mad Tahir heard the petition, filed by Ghulam Mur­taza, while Barrister Gohar appeared in person.

The court observed that Barrister Gohar could have submitted his response in writing.

The PTI leader told the court his party did not cla­im ownership of the X ac­­c­ount in question. However, citing a change in circumstances, he sought additional time to submit a detailed response.

Meanwhile, Judicial Magistrate Shaista Kundi issued arrest warrants for the accused who failed to appear in cases registered against the PTI founder and others in connection with the 2014 sit-in.

Mr Khan could not be produced in court as he is currently incarcerated in Adiala jail. The magistrate then adjourned proceedings till Nov 25 and directed that evidence be presented at the next hearing.

title: HRCP report paints grim picture of minority rights
text:
• Laments non-formation of national commission despite legislation being in place• Recommends reviewing school curricula to counter bigotry, promote inclusivity• Calls on Khyber Pakhtunkhwa to raise marriage age to 18 years, stresses need to curb hate speech

LAHORE: The Human Rights Commission of Pakistan (HRCP) warned that religious minorities continue to face violations of fundamental rights, including the misuse of blasphemy laws, forced marriages and conversions, and discriminatory practices, despite recent legislative measures aimed at protecting them.

In its seventh annual report on freedom of religion or belief, released on Thursday, the commission welcomed the passage of the National Commission for Minorities Act 2025 and laws in Punjab and Balochistan raising the minimum marriageable age to 18. However, it noted that the National Commission for Minorities had yet to be constituted, raising questions about the government’s commitment to implementing the legislation.

The report said hundreds of people accused of blasphemy remained in legal limbo, while alleged perpetrators of an organised entrapment network had yet to be investigated. It also documented attacks on the Ahmadi community, including two extremist attacks in Chenab Nagar, and increasingly overt attempts to exclude Ahmadis from public and commercial life.

Similarly, girls belonging to Christian and Hindu communities continued to face abductions and forced marriages, compounded by poverty and inadequate police responses, the report said. Discriminatory employment practices, the ‘distortion’ of school curricula, and the marginalisation of minority concerns in mainstream media further undermine the principle of equal citizenship, it added.

At the report’s launch, HRCP Director Farah Zia warned that the state’s approach to religious minorities was becoming increasingly exclusionary. Minority rights defender Nabila Feroz Bhatti highlighted the case of Kamran Gill, a Christian medical practitioner from Sheikhupura, whose dispensary was set ablaze by a mob on Oct 9 following allegations that he had shared blasphemous content on social media. HRCP Punjab vice-chair Raja Ashraf said blasphemy accusations had become a means of exploiting and endangering vulnerable people.

Community representative Amir Mahmood drew attention to restrictions on Ahmadis’ freedom of expression and assembly, recalling that the community’s last public gathering had taken place more than 40 years ago.

Former HRCP chairperson Hina Jilani highlighted the institutional nature of discrimination against minorities, saying: “Democracy should have no concept of ‘minority’ and ‘majority’.”

The report called on the federal government to implement the National Commission for Minorities Act without further delay by constituting the commission, framing its rules and appointing its chairperson and members in accordance with the law.

It urged federal and provincial governments to publish annual, disaggregated data on blasphemy cases, mob violence, forced conversion complaints and prison conditions to improve transparency and enable independent scrutiny of official claims.

The HRCP also called on Khyber Pakhtunkhwa to enact legislation setting the minimum marriageable age at 18 for both men and women, bringing the province in line with the laws recently adopted in Punjab and Balochistan.

It recommended prompt legal action against individuals and groups inciting violence, mandatory training for police and investigative agencies, including the Federal Investigation Agency, on freedom of religion or belief, and stronger safeguards for human rights defenders, lawyers and journalists working on minority rights.

The report further called for an end to discriminatory recruitment practices that confine many religious minorities to sanitation work and urged an overhaul of the Evacuee Trust Property Board to make it more transparent, accountable, and representative of minority communities.

It recommended that the federal government constitute an inquiry commission under the Pakistan Commission of Inquiry Act 2017 to examine findings of the Punjab Police Special Branch and the National Commission for Human Rights in October 2024.

The report also called for regular monitoring of seminaries linked to allegations of forced conversions and underage marriages, and recommended that religious conversions take place in court or in the presence of a government official.

Emphasising the need to curb hate speech, the HRCP urged authorities to take legal action against incitement to violence, particularly on social media, while respecting the freedom of speech guaranteed under Article 19 of the Constitution.

It called for improvements in pol­ice intelligence gathering, crowd con­­trol and community policing to prevent mob violence, as well as effective departmental accountability mechanisms to address corruption within law enforcement agencies.

The report recommended reviewing school curricula to counter religious bigotry and promote inclusivity and pluralism, operationalising provincial research centres envisaged under countering violent extremism laws, and keeping interfaith committees active throughout the year.

It also urged authorities to prevent pressure from bar associations and religious groups from influencing police and district administrations to act against particular sects or minority communities.

The HRCP called for full implementation of the Supreme Court’s 2014 judgement on religious freedoms, protection of minority places of worship and the reopening of Ahmadi places of worship closed on grounds of alleged threats to public order.

Given the severity of blasphemy charges, it recommended that investigations under Section 295C of the Pakistan Penal Code be conducted by senior-ranking officials. It also called for public awareness campaigns explaining sensitive laws carrying capital punishment, the methods used in alleged entrapment schemes in the digital age and developments in cyber laws.

The report stressed that mainstr­eam media should represent all segments of society, particularly marginalised groups, and stated that no place of worship should be demolished without a clear court order issued after hearing both sides.

title: Trump shuts down Hegseth plan to livestream execution
text:
WASHINGTON: President Donald Trump scrapped plans to livestream the execution of the former Army major who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, overruling Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth on Thursday after the proposal drew opposition from Republicans, religious leaders and the public.

The reversal ended a plan to broadcast Nidal Hasans Dec 3 firing-squad execution. It also marked a rare public disagreement between Trump and one of the presidents closest allies, although the Pentagon said the two were completely aligned.

Hegseth had announced plans to livestream the execution at the Fort Hood military base in Texas, the site of Hasan’s 2009 attack. No other country is known to televise or livestream judicial executions.

Trump and his advisers had been unaware of the livestream plan, said a White House official. “I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan but, many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device,” Trump wrote in a social media post.  “He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed.”  The families of Hasan’s victims will be able to view the execution in person if they so choose, as is standard at US executions.

Some of Trump’s fellow Republicans, including Vice President JD Vance, as well as religious leaders had expressed everything from doubts to outright condemnation of the Pentagon’s livestream plan. Opinion polls showed a majority of Americans opposed livestreaming it. Archbishop Timothy Broglio, who oversees the spiritual care of Catholic members of the US armed forces, also raised objections, while Pope Leo condemned capital punishment in all its forms.

An attorney representing Hasan could not immediately be reached for comment, and it was unclear if the scheduled Dec 3 execution date would be delayed by legal challenges. It was Trump’s first major public split with Hegseth, a Trump ally. But it was unclear whether the split would politically imperil Hegseth given their strong ties. In a statement, the Pentagon said Trump spoke with Hegseth about the decision before announcing it on Truth Social.

“The Secretary supports the President’s decision, and they are completely aligned,” chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement. Capital punishment in the US already was facing renewed scrutiny after Christa Pike, convicted of murder in the 1990s, survived two lethal injections in a failed execution attempt by Tennessee last month that left her badly injured and requiring hospitalisation.

A military jury convicted Hasan, a former US Army psychiatrist, of premeditated murder for fatally shooting 13 unarmed soldiers and wounding 32 others in a medical facility at the vast base. Law enforcement shot Hasan during his rampage, paralysing him from the waist down, and he now uses a wheelchair.

Hegseth had said the broadcasting of the execution was needed to ensure that people understand that  “there’s serious consequences for these types of things.”
