title: Bones from Iraqi cave hint at violence and compassion in Neanderthals
text:
The bones of a Neanderthal from a cave in Iraq’s Kurdistan region are offering evidence of both violence and compassion in the closest evolutionary cousins of our species, exhibiting a wound apparently from a fatal spear attack as well as signs of an earlier nonfatal injury that may have elicited kindly care.

Researchers have discovered at Shani­d­ar Cave in the Zagros Mountains of nort­hern Iraq a partial skeleton of a Nean­derthal, aged in the mid-40s, that included a left shoulder blade, or scapula, with a circular hole six-tenths of an inch wide indicative of a deeply penetrating stab.

The bones of this individual, who they call Shanidar A, were unearthed from under about 25 feet of rocks and sediment inside the cave and date to about 75,000 years ago. The researchers were unable to determine Shanidar A’s sex.

The researchers said the injury’s shape suggests it was caused by a forceful thrust using a sharpened wooden spear, a type of weapon Neanderthals are known to have used, rather than a spear with a stone tip. It was a weapon employed in hunting large mammals that were an important food source.

“The spear would have gone through the skin and major muscles, especially the pectoralis, as well as the ribcage and muscles between the ribs, and the lung,” said biological anthropologist Emma Pomeroy of the University of Cambridge in England, lead author of the study published on Thursday in the journal Scientific Reports.

“The location could be like the kind of ‘heart shot’ hunters use to kill animals quickly by puncturing the heart, but that is a bit speculative.”

title: What options does Indian law provide for CEC’s removal?
text:
AMID growing calls for the resignation of India’s top election official Gyanesh Kumar for alleged voter roll manipulation, a key issue has come to the fore: the process of the chief election commissioner’s appointment, resignation and termination. The campaign to remove Gyanesh Kumar from office began after a newspaper report alleged that he was responsible for removing the names of 130 million voters from India’s electoral rolls — a figure slightly higher than Bangladesh’s entire voting population.

While the Congress Party, India’s “cockroach” youth movement and others demand Kumar’s resignation, which is simple enough, Kumar’s removal from office is a lengthy and complicated affair, similar to the removal of a Supreme Court judge.

Article 324 of the Indian constitution, whi­ch deals with the Election Commission, outlines the procedures for removal of the election chief. Article 324 (5) stipulates that the top election official shall not be removed fr­­om office “except in like manner and on the like grounds as a Judge of the Supreme Court”.

In India, the CEC is appointed under the Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023. The CEC is appointed by the president.

The law stipulates that people who are serving or have served in positions equivalent to a secretary to the Indian government will be eligible. They also have to be “persons of integrity, who have knowledge of and experience in management and conduct of elections”. A search committee, led by the law minister, compiles a panel of five persons for consideration of the selection committee.

The election chief and commissioners are subsequently appointed by the president upon the recommendation of this selection committee, which currently consists of the prime minister, who serves as the chair, along with the leader of opposition in Lok Sabha and a minister as nominated by the prime minister.

The law governing their appointment, however, witnessed a significant change in 2023 where the constitution of the selection committee was changed. Earlier, the selection panel consisted of the prime minister, opposition leader and chief justice of India. The top judge was replaced by a union cabinet minister, for which Narendra Modi chose his home minister, Amit Shah.

Critics argue that this change increases executive influence over the appointment process, as two of the three members of the selection committee would be from the ruling party. As for resigning from office, it is a simple procedure where the election chief or any of the commissioners “may, at any time, by writing under his hand addressed to the president, resign his office”.

The election chief’s removal follows a quasi-judicial procedure in line with the procedure stipulated by the Judges Inquiry Act, 1968. Supreme Court and High Court judges can be removed on two grounds — proven misbehaviour and incapacity. A written notice must be signed by at least 100 members of the Lok Sabha or 50 members of the Rajya Sabha. The Lok Sabha Speaker or Rajya Sabha Chair examines the notice and available information, and decides to admit or refuse the motion.

If admitted, a committee is convened with one Supreme Court judge, one High Court judge and one distinguished legal expert. The election chief will have the right to defend against the allegation as the committee investigates. If the committee concludes that the charges are not proved, the motion is dropped, and the process ends.

If the committee finds that allegations are true, the report is submitted to the parliament. The motion to remove the election chief will have to carry a special majority (two-thirds of voters present and voting) in both houses, in order to pass. If the motion passes both houses, a formal address is presented to the president, who issues the official order of removal.

The election chief, Gyanesh Kumar has denied accusations of manipulating the voter list during an exercise to verify India’s one billion voters.

title: UN chief urges nations to end ‘war on nature’
text:
PARIS: UN chief Antonio Guterres said on Thursday that the  “war on nature has not yet ended” as he launched a report showing the world was falling short of its biodiversity commitments. Nations will assess progress and pitfalls toward a 2030 goal to stop the destruction of nature when they meet in Armenia next week for the UN biodiversity negotiations.

Nearly 200 countries joined the landmark  “Paris Agreement for Nature” four years ago but have been slow to act on its objectives. The pact laid out 23 targets for halting and reversing nature loss by 2030, including reducing pollution, protecting threatened species and conserving 30pc of the world’s land and oceans.

But many of these targets are off track, said Guterres as he launched a global report spotlighting the gaps between ambition and action. “It’s not all bad news... There is progress, but not enough. We are far from what is necessary,” he told reporters in the Armenian capital Yerevan where the COP17 talks start on Monday.

“The report shows that many of the critical elements of progress... are still missing in action”.

title: 7 sailors missing after drones hit two ships near Romania
text:
BUCHAREST: Rescuers searched on Thursday for seven missing sailors after drones struck two chemical tankers near Romania’s Black Sea coast, setting them ablaze and raising fresh security concerns along a vital shipping route used by Ukraine.

Romanian President Nicusor Dan said the two ships had been struck by drones but declined to say whether Russia was responsible, while a Nato military source said the drones came from Russia. “The drones that caused the fires on board two tankers inside Romanian territorial waters were of Russian origin,” the Nato source said.

The two vessels were anchored near the mouth of the Sulina canal leading into the Danube River, a major export route used by Ukraine as Russia has repeatedly attacked Ukraine’s Black Sea ports. One was inside Romanian territorial waters and the other just outside. The missing crew were among 12 sailors aboard the San Marino-flagged tanker Wine Trader, which was hit 13 nautical miles southeast of the Sulina canal, one mile outside Romanian waters. Five crew members were rescued, Romanian officials said.

The second vessel, the Comoros-flagged chemical and oil tanker Yara J, caught fire after being struck 8-10 miles southeast of Sulina inside Romanian waters late on Wednesday. All crew were safe.

The attacks are the latest in a series of strikes on commercial shipping in the western Black Sea. At least five other cargo vessels have been hit near the coasts of Romania and neighbouring Nato member Bulgaria over the past 10 days, with at least 23 sailors reported missing or dead. Those attacks occurred outside Nato territorial waters.

“The situation in the Black Sea is serious,” Romania’s Dan said. “Commercial ships are being attacked and sunk. Seafarers killed, injured, and missing, very close to the shores of Romania and Bulgaria. Lives, global trade, and critical infrastructure are at stake.”

The interior ministry said it had sent two Black Hawk helicopters to the search and rescue mission, as we­­ll as two ships with medical staff on board. “At the moment, the rescue cannot be done safely because of very big waves,” it said in a statement.

Nato said in a statement it was in contact with Romanian officials. It added two other vessels had been targeted in the Black Sea overnight, Marshall Islands-flagged bulk carrier Sea Destiny inside Romanian waters and Tanzanian-flagged tanker Dania J, moored in the Ukrainian Danube port of Izmail. It did not mention casualties.

“Nato will continue to work closely with our Allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defence posture as needed,” Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte said after meeting Dan and Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev on Thursday.

Romania shares a 614-km border with Ukraine, much of it along the Danube, and has repeatedly reported Russian drone incursions into its airspace since the start of Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The escalating attacks on Black Sea shipping have heightened concerns over grain exports from the region.

title: Zelensky must go, says Musk after SpaceX satellite dispute
text:
WASHINGTON: Tech billionaire Elon Musk called on Wednesday for Volodymyr Zelensky to  “go” as Ukraine’s leader, after insisting any disruption to the war-torn country’s use of his satellite communications system was the fault of the US government, not his company.

The comments came as Kyiv raised doubts over US support for Ukraine in its war with Russia, accusing Washington this week of helping Moscow by failing to warn it of incoming missile strikes and hobbling Kyiv’s military response through changes to the SpaceX-designed system it uses for communications.

“And so the slaughter continues,” Musk wrote on X.  “Time for Zelensky to go.” Musk earlier said that  “any limits on speed or usage” of his SpaceX company’s Starshield systems were  “decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” referring to US President Donald Trump.

He drew a distinction between Starshield, which Ukraine relies on for battlefield communications, and the parallel Starlink civilian satellite system, which Kyiv also deploys but is not allowed to use for offensive operations.

Musk was responding to a post on X by Ukraine’s former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov, who said that  “Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 160 km/h is being restored,” but that  “removing Starshield’s speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine’s defense.”

Ukrainian defense officials have suggested Washington is behind slower speeds reported on some internet terminals that help the country’s military hit Russian-occupied territory and operate interceptor drones.

title: Deadly classrooms
text:
AT LEAST 30 children, most of them younger than 13, and a teacher have died in Peshawar after the roof of their private schoolcollapsedduring morning classes. Dozens more were injured, some critically.

The victims had arrived at the Al Khair school expecting an ordinary day. Instead, rescue workers spent hours searching through rubble as parents gathered outside. Police say the building was structurally weak and its roof overloaded with additional construction. The owner has been arrested, while an inquiry is under way. These preliminary findings demand scrutiny. So do reports that concerns about the building’s condition had previously been raised. In June, 14 children died when the roof of a tuition centrecollapsedin Lahore’s Kahna area. Two days later, another schoolroof collapsein Baghbanpura killed an eight-year-old. Three incidents in a few months should be enough to force an examination of the places where Pakistan’s children are taught.

Across the country, schools and tuition centres operate in buildings ill-suited to accommodating large numbers of pupils. In crowded urban neighbourhoods, houses are converted into classrooms, sometimes with additional floors, makeshift rooms, and roofs carrying more weight than they were designed to support.

Yet questions about construction quality, structural approvals, and inspections are too often left unanswered until a disaster occurs. The Lahore inquiry found that the Kahna tuition centre operated from an unregistered residential house. Peshawar presents a troubling contrast: according to the KP private schools regulator, Al Khair was registered in March, but technical personnel were absent from its inspection.

If a school can receive registration without a structural assessment, what assurance does that certificate provide? Investigators must establish whether alterations were authorised, who inspected the premises, and whether warnings were received and ignored. They must also examine the regulators’ role, not merely the decisions of school management.

The KP authorities’ decision to establish district-level committees to inspect private school buildings is welcome, but its value will depend on what follows. The committees have been instructed to examine buildings, identify hazards, and submit reports within three days. Authorities must make the findings public, close premises posing danger, and require independent engineering clearance before they reopen. Similar checks are needed across every province, including at tuition centres and schools operating inside residential properties. Building permission, school registration, and periodic safety certification should be linked, with clear responsibility assigned to qualified inspectors. Owners who make dangerous alterations must face consequences, as must officials found to have neglected their duties. Parents should not have to become structural engineers to judge whether their children are safe at school. After so many deaths, another round of condolences and inquiries without enforcement would be an intolerable response.

title: Diplomatic options
text:
AS Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthi movement continue totrade fire, and theUS-Iran waris locked in a stalemate, regional states continue to stress the need for a diplomatic solution to the conflicts in both theatres. Numerous attempts have been made in the past to find a negotiatedoff-rampin both conflicts, but they have met with little success.

Regional states know that the alternative to talks — a fully fledged war on both fronts — will bring immeasurable destruction to the Gulf, the Red Sea and the surrounding areas. The need for diplomacy was stressed during Omani Foreign Minister Badr al-Busaidi’svisitto Pakistan on Wednesday. Though the visit was of a bilateral nature, the regional situation was high on the agenda, with Oman’s top diplomat reiterating that “diplomacy is the only way forward”.

Both Pakistan and Oman have played integral roles in trying to find anegotiatedsettlement to the US-Iran dispute, while the sultanate is also a key link between the Saudis and the Houthis. Both Pakistan and Oman know that any further escalation either in the Gulf or in Yemen will destabilise the whole region.

With regard to the Yemeni conflict, while Pakistan has pledged to stand “shoulder to shoulder” with Saudi Arabia, the prospect of a long war of attrition involving the kingdom and its allies, and the pro-Iran Houthis, is in no one’s interest. The goal, therefore, should be a renewed ceasefire, which promises Saudi security and an end to the Yemeni civil war. Pakistan, Oman and other regional states should concentrate on achieving this goal.

Where Iran is concerned, it is likely that the US will make its next move after themidterm electionsin early November. However, media reports that America plans on dropping the ‘mother of all bombs’ on Iranian energy and nuclear sites should be a matter of concern for all. America’s aggression has failed to make Iran capitulate, and it is hard to see what more violence will achieve, other than perpetuating chaos in the region.

What is needed is a holistic ceasefire that addresses all fronts — Iran, Yemen, Lebanon — along with a long-term peace between the US and Iran. The US must also refrain from initiating more wars in the Middle East, along with reining in its bloodthirsty ally Israel.

title: Hunger in Pakistan
text:
PAKISTAN’S position as the country most affected by hunger in South Asia is not surprising. An economy battered by weather-related disasters, persistent food inflation, weak growth, terrorism, poverty, and joblessness cannot ensure that its people eat enough and well. The findings of the 2026 Global Hunger Index reveal the inadequacy of our economic, agricultural and social policies. Food insecurity is not simply a problem of inadequate agricultural production, but also of access and affordability. The availability of food in the market matters little to families whose incomes cannot keep pace with the prices. Weak farm productivity, inadequate water management, poor storage, post-harvest losses, and flawed market arrangements have long undermined the food system. High input costs, disrupted livelihoods, and falling purchasing power have made nutritious food difficult for poorer households to afford.

Climate change compounds these pressures. Repeated floods destroy crops, livestock, homes, and rural livelihoods. Droughts, erratic rainfall, and rising temperatures threaten harvests. Farmers face risks alongside costly agricultural inputs and uncertain returns. The resulting losses push up food prices, reduce rural incomes, and increase dependence on relief. Policies that fail to encourage investment in modern farming, improve yields or protect farmers’ incentives leave production vulnerable. The human cost is particularly severe for children. The GHI notes that undernourishment has worsened since 2018, and child wasting has moved towards the high threshold. Persistent malnutrition damages physical growth, cognitive development, and future earning capacity. Hunger, therefore, perpetuates poverty and poor productivity across generations. The government must move beyond temporary subsidies. Social protection must reach households that cannot afford basic nutrition, particularly during disasters and price shocks. Besides productive agriculture, climate-resilient infrastructure, better water management, reduced food wastage, and stronger rural employment, lasting progress demands sustained investment in maternal and child nutrition, clean water and primary healthcare.

title: Equities extend overnight recovery rally
text:
KARACHI: Shrugging off the prevailing regional and political turmoil, which poses serious risks to macroeconomic stability amid inflationary pressures stemming from elevated oil prices and higher energy costs, the Pakistan Stock Exchange (PSX) on Thursday managed to sustain gains above the 166,000 level as equity investors continued their value-hunting for the second straight session, helping the benchmark KSE-100 index close higher.

Topline Securities Ltd said the index closed higher on Thursday, gaining 768.66 points, or 0.46 per cent, to settle at 166,186.17. It traded between 165,613 and 166,877, sustaining positive momentum throughout the session amid renewed buying interest.

The market’s recovery was supported by selective accumulation in key index-heavy stocks after the recent correction. However, investor sentiment remained cautious amid fluctuations in international oil prices, developments in the Middle East and locally, domestic macroeconomic indicators, and institutional fund flows.

Index sustains gains above 166,000 level on value-hunting

Ali Najib, Deputy Head of Trading at Arif Habib Ltd, said the PSX recorded another positive session, reclaiming the 166,000 level.

The market opened on a positive note and maintained its upward momentum throughout the session. However, profit-taking in select stocks at higher levels trimmed some of the gains.

On the geopolitical front, continued Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, targeting airports and oil facilities, heightened regional security risks.

Pakistan Telecom­muni­cation Company, Fauji Fertiliser, Systems Ltd, Hub Power, Oil and Gas Development Company, Meezan Bank, Lucky Cement, Habib Bank, Pakistan Petroleum and United Bank collectively contributed 560 points to the index.

Investor participation weakened, with trading volume dipping 11.65pc to 517.6 million shares. However, turnover rose 17.42pc to Rs23.5 billion. Cnergyico PK led the volume chart with 62.8 million shares.

Analysts believe that sus­­tained gains above 166,000, supported by broad-based buying, signal a constructive near-term outlook. However, profit-taking near the intraday high, signalling that market participants are incli­ned to “sell on strength,” and escalating Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia may keep investor sentiment cautious amid heightened geopolitical risks.

title: Textile exports rise
text:
ISLAMABAD: Pakis­tan’s textile and clothing exports rose 5.26 per cent to $5.026 billion in the first quarter of 2026-27 from $4.775bn in the same period last year.

The marginal rise in export proceeds was attributed to elevated input costs, which eroded exporters’ competitiveness, and external shocks that disrupted shipments, according to data from the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics released on Thursday.

Textile exporters have already warned the government that exports could slow further in the second quarter if no corrective measures are taken.

Two major setbacks mainly contributed to slowing exports — suspension of trade with Afghanistan since October 2025 and falling exports to the Middle East due to the prevailing war in the region, especially the United Arab Emirates.

PBS data showed readymade garment exports surged 15.69pc in value and 17.38pc in quantity during July-September FY27, while knitwear rose 4.14pc in value but fell 0.46pc in quantity. By contrast, bedwear dipped 0.07pc in value and 0.71pc in quantity.

Pakistan’s oil import bill rose 6.50pc in 1QFY27 to $4.02bn from $3.77bn a year ago. Data showed import of crude oil jumped 23.10pc in value, with a decline of 6.87pc in quantity, indicating that the higher value of crude oil is due to rising international oil prices.

title: State Bank of Pakistan's reserves rise
text:
KARACHI: The State Bank of Pakistan’s foreign exchange reserves rose by $16 million to $21.469 billion during the week ended on Oct 9, reported the central bank on Thursday.

The SBP has maintained a record-high increase in reserves since inflows of $3bn from the sale of Eurobonds, despite a rising trade deficit.

The country’s total rese­rves reached $26.863bn during the week, including $5.393bn held by commercial banks.

title: UNDP warns of poverty surge after Iran war
text:
BANGKOK: Millions could be thrown into poverty by surging energy costs, the impact of an intense El Nino phenomenon and higher interest rates, with vulnerable countries being pushed to the brink by repeated crises, the UN’s development chief told AFP.

Global fuel prices have soared since the United States launched its war on Iran in late February, with Tehran’s retaliations against Washington’s Gulf allies curtailing major oil and natural gas supplies.

Fiscal deficits and debt-to-GDP ratios around the world have ballooned since the 2008 global financial crisis, with governments firefighting against a series of shocks including the pandemic and wars in Ukraine and the Middle East.

Speaking on the sidelines of the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, UN Development Programme (UNDP) head Alexander de Croo said many developing countries had responded to the current spike in energy prices with blanket subsidies, but a succession of crises had left them with limited resources to keep that up.

Says energy shock could push 130m into poverty

“You have to repair your roof while at the same time your home is on fire,” he told AFP, adding governments in the developing world did not have time to rebuild buffers or resolve previous shocks before being hit by new crises.

The IMF warned this week that while global growth had held up in the face of the energy crisis, that resilience was highly dependent on the boom in AI technology investments, and poorer countries not exposed to that were still struggling.

IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva had warned that “winter is coming” — an allusion to popular fantasy book series Game of Thrones —implying that a cataclysm was around the corner if the world did not prepare for it.

And De Croo added: “Some countries have a well-insulated house with money in the bank. Other countries have a house without a roof and no money in the bank.

“We’re stumbling from one crisis into the other, and what countries need is some space, and some time, and access to financing.” Not getting the response right could be devastating. The UNDP warned in a new report that about 130 million people were at risk of being pushed into poverty this year if energy and food price increases were fully passed on without subsidies.

People in South and East Asia and sub-Saharan Africa are at particular risk, the agency said.‘Difficult to manage’

With advanced economies seeing bond yields surge — owing to elevated inflation expectations, surging debt ratios and AI capital-raising activities — global borrowing costs have been rising.

That in turn, de Croo warned, had tightened space for developing countries to access the capital they needed to combat the shocks, with rising interest rates feeding into increasing debt payments.

According to UNDP, the median developing country now spends about 9.5 percent of government revenue on interest payments — the highest in a quarter of a century, and more than three times that of high-income countries.

“It starts to be a difficult situation to manage, and it takes away all their margin for policy,” de Croo said.

The former Belgian prime minister said he would spend the week in Bangkok — where world economic policy leaders have gathered since Monday — pushing for advanced economies and multilateral agencies to invest in economic growth, resilience and job creation in the developing world.

title: Returns filing date extended to 31st
text:
ISLAMABAD: The Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) has extended the deadline for filing income tax returns to October 31.

An official announcement on Thursday said all taxpayers can now file their returns for tax year 2026 by the extended deadline. The deadline, originally set for Sept 30, was first extended by two weeks to Oct 15.

Meanwhile, the FBR received 943,000 new tax returns during the first extension of the filing deadline by Oct 15.

Total returns filed through Oct 14 reached 6.710 million, compared with 4.993m returns filed over the corresponding period last year, an increase of 34.38pc.

Until Sept 30, total returns received were 5.767m, up from 3.980m last year, an increase of 45pc.

FBR receives record 6.71 million returns by Oct 14; non-salaried filers surge by 46 per cent

As a result, total tax paid on returns up to Oct 14 stood at Rs66.81 billion, about 14.61pc above last year’s Rs58.29bn.

Non-salaried filers led the 2026 tax year. Returns filed by non-salaried individuals, a category that covers traders, shopkeepers, professionals, and the self-employed, rose 46.35pc, from 3.038m to 4.446m. This marks a significant shift in the filing of tax returns.

Salaried returns rose by 16.16pc to 2.178 m in tax year 2026 from 1.875m the previous year. Returns from associations of persons, including partnerships, rose 14.64pc to 74,278 in tax year 2026, up from 64,789 in the previous tax year.

The one category that has moved in the other direction is companies. Only 11,089 company returns have been filed so far, down from 14,292 by this date last year, a decline of 22.41pc.

FBR officials describe this decline in corporate returns filings as a matter of timing. Many companies, they say, held back in the expectation that the filing date would be extended further. However, a surge was recorded in tax payments with returns.

The FBR attributes the overall rise in tax return filings to three factors. First, data from banks, property registries, vehicle registration records, and withholding statements are now matched against tax returns to identify people with taxable capacity who have not filed.

The second is a simpler return that enables most salaried individuals and small businesses to file without professional assistance. The third is enforcement: those who fail to file now face restrictions on major economic transactions.

title: Two firms ink MoU for Rs20bn gas investment
text:
ISLAMABAD: Shaheen Energy (Pvt) Ltd (SEPL) and Anton Oilfield Services Group, China, have signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to explore significant investment opportunities in Pakistan’s gas sector under the government’s 35pc third-party gas sale framework.

Both companies intend to undertake an investment programme of about Rs20 billion over the next three to five years, focusing on Pakistan’s policy reforms that have opened new opportunities in the domestic gas market and upstream gas sector (EPC) projects, according to a statement by Shaheen Energy.

Under the amended Pet­­roleum (Exploration & Production) Policy 2012, exploration and production (E&P) companies can sell up to 35pc of their share of pipeline-specification gas to third-party buyers holding a licence from the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority through a competitive process.

The policy amendment was introduced through a statutory regulatory order in 2024. The framework represents a significant shift in Pakistan’s gas sector, supporting greater commercial flexibility for eligible gas producers and creating opportunities for private investment in gas processing, transportatio­­­n, and supply infrastructure.

The Karachi-based SEPL is one of the leading ene­rgy companies in the country, engaged in developing and operating low-pressure gas facilities for the processing and utilisation of natural gas and flare gas. The company specialises in gas processing, cle­aning, purificati­on, dehydration and compression, making gas suitable for supply to industrial and commercial consumers.

title: PM rejects LPG auction sans legal cover, policy
text:
ISLAMABAD: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has rejected a move by the Petroleum Division to auction liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) produced by state-owned entities (SOEs) in the absence of a legal and policy framework.

The prime minister suggested there should be a comprehensive policy change, backed by legal and regulatory framework, before any transaction is executed so that unnecessary controversies were avoided, an official toldDawn.

PM Shehbaz declined to approve any interim measures. As a result, the simultaneous auctions conducted by three major LPG producers in the public sector on Aug 10 would not go ahead, he added.

The approval of the bidding results was estimated to jack up LPG prices by at least 15 per cent on top of higher winter prices. The proposal would have linked the producer price of locally produced LPG to import parity and widened the margins allowed to marketing companies and distributors.

Approval of bidding process would have ramped up prices by 15pc

It would have had a net impact of Rs77, 000 per tonne, or around Rs900 for a domestic cylinder of 11.8kg.

A domestic cylinder changes hands at around Rs5,000 against the OGRA’s notified maximum of Rs3,296, a premium of roughly Rs1,700, or 52pc. This is mainly due to supply squeeze on two fronts and the authorities’ refusal to address the issue.

Land route volumes through Taftan border remain negligible, while LPG totalling over 25,000 tonnes is backed up at Rahimdan, near Gwadar. Each bowser now waits about a month to be decanted and cleared at the Gwadar terminal, a delay industry officials say has pushed freight costs from $100 a tonne to $400.

The closure of the Strait of Hormuz has curtailed imports, leaving Oman as the principal alternative source. Correspondence seen by Dawn suggests that the Foreign Office, at the Petroleum Division’s request, had approached Oman for cargoes from OQ Trading, the state-owned supplier.

Insiders suggest that before the petroleum authorities could make a timely decision, OQ Trading instead committed its available volumes to a single private buyer on commercial terms. This is feeding the black market and price escalation in the open market.

Informed sources said the storage at both LPG terminals at Port Qasim was full to capacity, meaning that the shortage was an artificial phenomenon given the fact that stocks should be on the daily reporting dashboard of the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra). Weak enforcement is also a cause, they added.

The sources said police had reported loaded LPG bowsers parked in some areas, creating security and safety risks on highways.

On the instructions of the petroleum division, the three SOEs carried out auctions on Aug 10 simultaneously. The highest bidder offered Rs205 million for supply of a lot over three years. One lot was of five tonnes a day.

The country’s total LPG requirement fluctuates between 1.4 and two million tonnes. More than half of it is imported.

Some existing LPG stakeholders, fearing loss of business and market competition, are already in the court against the bidding process on grounds that existing policies and rules provide no such arrangement.

The Petroleum Division and its entities are believed to have held multiple sessions with the Attorney General for Pakistan to push for speedy judicial proceedings.

Under the directives of Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik, the four public sector entities — Oil & Gas Development Company Ltd, Pakistan Petroleum Limited, Pak-Arab Refinery Company and Govt Holdings Pvt Limited — were required to offer standardised lots of five tonnes each on pilot basis to replace “the existing quota-based system”.

The signature bonus adds close to 15pc on top of the last price notified by Ogra at around Rs3,296 per 11.8kg cylinder.

title: Sindh woos Chinese investors
text:
SHANGHAI: Sindh Chief Minister Syed Murad Ali Shah has made a strong case for Chinese investment in the province, highlighting its strategic location, extensive sea and air connectivity, competitive labour costs and skilled workforce.

Addressing the second Sindh Invest­ment Conference, held in Shanghai after a 12-year hiatus, Mr Shah said the moot would usher in a new era of Chinese investment, job creation, and industrial modernisation in the province.

Mr Shah also presented the Dhabeji Special Economic Zone as a flagship opportunity for Chinese and other international investors seeking a cost-effective base for manufacturing and export-oriented businesses.

The proposed industrial clusters at Dhabeji include automotive and auto parts, light engineering, chemicals and pharmaceuticals, consumer electronics, steel and foundries, warehousing, construction materials, textiles and garments.

34 MoUs signed at Shanghai moot held after 12 years

The day-long moot was attended by around 400 delegates, including investors, business leaders and representatives of Chinese companies and financial institutions.

The conference featured presentations on major sectors, networking sessions and the signing of 34 memoranda of understanding involving government-to-government (G2G) and business-to-business (B2B) cooperation.

The chief minister said Sindh was ready to become a natural partner for Chinese investors seeking scale, connectivity and government-backed support. He said the provincial government was committed to facilitating foreign investment and ensuring that agreements translated into practical projects.

“Sindh offers a cost-effective environment for investment that compares favourably with many countries around the world,” Mr Shah said, emphasising the province’s potential to attract foreign direct investment and strengthen international trade partnerships.

He said Sindh combines Pakistan’s largest commercial city, two major seaports, extensive industrial capacity, substantial energy and mineral resources, a large agricultural base and several investment platforms linked to the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor.

Speaking to the media after the conference, Mr Shah said the 12-year gap was used effectively to prepare Sindh’s infrastructure, policy framework, and workforce to absorb high-value international investments.

Highlighting the tangible outcomes of the five-day visit to China, Mr Shah announced that Sindh government entities and Chinese enterprises have signed 34 memoranda of understanding (MoUs), alongside numerous agreements between private-sector business entities from both sides.

He emphasised that these MoUs are not merely symbolic but are underpinned by rigorous prior groundwork, ensuring their swift translation into operational projects. Major sectors identified for enhanced bilateral cooperation include Thar Coal utilisation, electric vehicle (EV) manufacturing and the establishment of charging stations, renewable energy (wind and solar), modern agriculture, and digital transformation.

Unveiling futuristic economic plans, the chief minister noted immense potential for cooperation in Artificial Intelli­gence, large data processing, and establishing state-of-the-art data centres.

The chief minister said Chinese manufacturers could produce goods in Sindh, use the province’s energy and industrial inputs, and transport finished products through Karachi Port and Port Qasim.

He also highlighted Sindh’s 350-kilometre coastline, access to major trade routes, and proximity to markets in Central Asia, the Middle East, and Africa.
